World.title: Marine microplastic pollution: How scientists detect it | Euronews Tech Talks
World.content:
The sea holds many secrets that are invisible to the naked eye when viewed from the shore: rare species, complex ecosystems and, sadly, loads of litter.

 

According to the United Nations, each year 52 million tonnes of plastic waste enter the ocean, resulting in an estimated 24 trillion microplastic particles.

Microplastics, tiny fragments of plastics less than 5 millimetres in diameter, can be found both in the depths and on the surface of the water, disrupting ecosystems in ways scientists are still trying to understand.

But how do microplastics get into the sea? What technologies can be used to identify them? And what impact do they have on marine species?

To answer these and more questions, Euronews Tech Talks visited the Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ) in Ostend, on the Belgian coast. Here, a research group led by senior researcher Ana Catarino investigates marine microplastics, collecting data directly from the North Sea.

Marine microplastics pollution, climate change and risks

Plastics can enter the ocean in multiple ways: pieces of fishing nets that accidentally detach, litter coming from malfunctioning waste management systems, and so on.

Specifically, microplastics polluting the ocean can be divided into two categories: primary microplastics and secondary microplastics.

The former category comprises elements like nurdles, tiny plastic fragments designed for industrial purposes; while the latter involves particles stemming from the degradation of macro litter due to waves, wind and exposure to sunlight.

The extent of microplastic pollution is, therefore, tied to climate change.

“So if we have more sunny days and higher UV radiation exposure and heat waves and changes of temperature that might, for example, impact the degradation of plastics that are stranded,” Catarino said.

The impact of microplastics on marine species is also closely linked to climate change. On their own, the microplastics ingested by a species may not pose a significant risk.

But if that species is already under stress due to rising sea temperatures, the consequences can be different. “These combined effects, they can be cumulative in the organism,” Catarino explained.

Methods to identify microplastics

Marine microplastics are difficult to identify and quantify due to their small dimensions, irregular shape, and, sometimes, different colours.

Despite these challenges, recognising microplastics is possible, and VLIZ’s postdoctoral researcher Nelle Meyers has worked on a semi-automated method to identify them.

This technique involves collecting a sample from the sea using a net, cleaning the sample of organic materials, and staining it with Nile Red before placing it under a microscope. A fluorescence colouration analysis is then run and its results are passed through two automated programmes that can identify whether a particle is a microplastic or not and what type of microplastic it is.

“We wanted to automate to speed up the whole process,” Meyers said. “We wrote a code so when you upload the picture, the image analysis is done automatically,” she continued.

Thanks to this semi-automated step and the use of a fluorescence microscope, which is relatively common in laboratories, Meyers claimed the technique is cost- and time-effective.

However, the method also presents some limitations, as it lacks information about the chemical composition of the particles and can determine only certain types of polymers.

Microplastics’ impact on marine species

Just as larger plastic debris is ingested by marine species, tiny plastic particles can also be consumed by smaller organisms, like plankton.

“They [microplastics] can also get their stomach, their gut clogged. And then they [small organisms] don't eat their nutrients, they don't eat their own food,” Catarino explained.

“And this is worrying because then it brings other issues because these organisms are not able to reproduce and their population will not strive, so it will be affected,” she said.

The specific effects of microplastics depend on multiple factors, including the marine species involved, the type of microplastics, and other stressors to which the species is exposed, such as changes in sea temperature, ocean acidification, and more.

“Sometimes it’s not just one issue or another, it’s the accumulation of all these effects that may be harmful to the organisms,” Catarino told Euronews Next.

World.title: Euronews in Cotignac: How a historic French village survived a night of wildfire
World.content:
Ash still covered the streets of Cotignac on Wednesday morning after a wildfire that broke out the previous afternoon tore through the medieval cliffside village in the heart of Provence, destroying nearly 60 homes and burning thousands of hectares across five communes overnight.

 

The fire started in a field near the village of Pontevès on Tuesday and spread rapidly northward, driven by wind and drought, before reaching Cotignac during the night.

By dawn it had burned through the nearby communes, bringing in more than 900 firefighters with reinforcements from across southern France, including Marseille's naval pompiers.

Four people were injured — two firefighters and two civilians. Around 500 residents were evacuated across the affected communes by Wednesday afternoon. Thousands of homes lost electricity, the majority in Cotignac itself.

The village, which regularly wins recognition as one of France's most beautiful and whose summer population swells from around 2,500 to nearly 10,000, was the hardest hit.

The Sanctuaire Notre-Dame de Grâces, a 16th-century pilgrimage site built on the spot where the Virgin Mary is said to have appeared in 1519, and the nearby Monastery of Saint-Joseph du Bessillon were evacuated and came within metres of the flames but survived.

Animals, both domestic and living in the nearby forests, also suffered throughout the night. Cattle trucks were seen being evacuated off the hills on Tuesday, while some residents told Euronews they lost horses in stables affected by the blaze overnight.

Wild boars or sangliers, which thrive across Provence in the hundreds of thousands, were spotted on the lower roads out of the village in broad daylight, running for their lives from the wildfire.

On Wednesday, teams of pompiers were still working to protect an entire field of horses in Correns, some 20 kilometres down the road from Cotignac.

Residents look on as smoke and fire approach the village of Pontignac, in Provence, south of France, 21 July 2026 Euronews

For residents who lived through the night, survival depended on quick decisions and often on the kindness of strangers.

Village resident Lolita Philippon described how an elderly relative had come close to being caught in the flames in the Caillades area.

"My ex-mother-in-law got stuck in the flames. She went back home to save her cats and put them in safety. She got stuck by the flames while getting out," Roubard told Euronews.

"Her sister got her back in the car. They wanted to leave together, but in the end they got stuck. She panicked and got out of the car."

The woman then took refuge in her neighbour's pool, Roubard said.

"I don't really know how she managed to contact her son, who came to rescue her, who contacted the firefighters. He got her out of the water, the firefighters came to help her, and they directed them to Le Val," she explained.

Many open doors to strangers

With official information slow to reach residents, the village's informal networks carried much of the weight of communication through the night.

"We all went to the centre of the village and watched the smoke roll over the hills from a huge fire that seemed to be right behind the village, and there wasn't a lot of information going around officially," another resident, John Michael Peck, told Euronews.

"We all found ourselves gathering in places known to us all where everyone would be and just exchanging information, because everyone wanted to know what to do, how close the fire was," Peck said.

"Everyone has a cousin or a friend who's a pompier around here. And so we all had first-hand information trickling down through the grapevine, essentially, and getting to the ears that needed to hear it."

Fire nears the outskirts of the village of Pontignac, in Provence, south of France, 21 July 2026 Euronews

That community network, he said, translated into practical help.

"A lot of people ended up opening their doors to strangers. Anyone who was in a location that was affected or ordered to evacuate came to the village and got filtered through the network of friends and relations and taken care of really well," Peck explained.

"The priests and the nuns came down from Notre-Dame, which had flames literally licking the stones behind it in the woods, and were able to easily find accommodation with strangers."

Peck said Lou Calen, an eco-resort with a Michelin Green-starred restaurant, opened its doors on Wednesday morning and gave breakfast to anyone who had been at the sanctuary.

He himself left for the home of a friend of a friend in Salernes. "I showed up with my cat and my best friend and his baby. They took us on like family."

"That's Cotignac," Peck concluded.

'They are completely lost'

The destruction has left some families with nothing. "When I went to work this morning, my colleague told me that his parents completely lost their house because of the fire last night in Cotignac," a second resident, Manon Roubard told Euronews.

"So they had to leave. And thanks to all the community, Carcès opened free places that people who had to leave could go," she pointed out.

"They went to Carcès. And one of their friends called them to tell them to come over and sleep for the night. So I could feel relief at least a little bit, but it was really painful for them."

"They are completely lost. It is really complicated for people like them — older people — who can lose everything," Roubard said.

Wildfire nearing the village of Les Arcs, in France, 21 July 2026 Euronews

The town of Carcès activated its emergency community plan and opened three reception facilities, including a gymnasium and the Château hall, to support evacuees from the affected area.

By Wednesday morning the fire was still active but less aggressive, according to the Var prefecture. The official assessment of damage to homes was continuing.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: US hits Iran as Houthis claim strikes on Saudi tankers

Published 07/23/2026 Published July 23, 2026 Yemen's Houthis says they targeted Saudi oil tankers in Red Sea

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement says it has targeted two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, escalating tensions around one of the world's key energy shipping routes.

The group identified the vessels as the Encelia and Layla, saying they were attacked with ballistic and cruise missiles for allegedly violating a Houthi naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, announced earlier this week.

A maritime security source told Reuters, the Saudi-flagged tanker Encelia sent a distress call after reporting it had been hit by a missile and caught fire near the Saudi port of Jizan.

Maritime security firm Vanguard and the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) also reported a tanker being struck by an unidentified projectile in the same area, causing a fire onboard. No casualties have been reported.

According to UKMTO, the ship’s master reported the incident approximately 70 nautical miles (130 kilometers) south-west of Al-Shuqaiq, Saudi Arabia.

Iran war: Analyzing the Houthi blockade against Saudi Arabia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Houthis also claimed to have targeted a second vessel, Layla, though that report has not been independently confirmed.

The attack comes days after the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi ports in the Red Sea, raising concerns about disruptions to global energy supplies. Ship-tracking data showed several tankers changing course on Wednesday following Houthi warnings to avoid Saudi ports.

World.title: Iran war: Trump threatens bridges over Hormuz Strait attacks
World.content:
Skip next section Signs of ships avoiding second choke point off Yemen after Houthi warnings: tracker data

07/22/2026 July 22, 2026 Signs of ships avoiding second choke point off Yemen after Houthi warnings: tracker data

Houthi supporters rallied in Sanaa in support of the announcement of a maritime blockade earlier this week [FILE: July 20, 2026] Image: Mohammed Hamoud/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Houthi threats to ships headed to or from Saudi Arabia's western shoreline could further impact commercial shipping, data trackers are warning.

The Houthis, who have de facto control over much of Yemen, have declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia and told ships to avoid the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the gateway to the Red Sea on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz. It provides access to western Saudi coastal cities like Jeddah and Yanbu.

Data provider Kpler said shipping in both waterways was "under pressure," saying traffic in both straits had fallen sharply.

Ship broker Clarksons issued a similar warning, saying four vessels had registered new courses on Wednesday, avoiding the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and heading north through the Suez Canal towards the Mediterranean instead.

"The threat of Houthi hostile actions against Saudi Arabia ... has begun to have an overall effect on tanker activity," Clarksons wrote. "There are reports of several tankers, having ​loaded in Saudi Arabia's Yanbu port in the Red Sea, that have shifted course towards the Suez Canal rather than sail south towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, while ​others are holding their positions waiting for further instruction."

For ships headed to places like India, Pakistan, Indonesia or Australia, doing this would add well over 10,000 nautical miles (more than 20,000 kilometers) and weeks at sea to the typical travel distance.

"Anything that restricts shipping through the Red Sea would be problematic for the same reasons that the Strait of Hormuz is problematic," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on the sidelines of a regional summit in the Philippines on Wednesday.

Pakistan's Foreign Ministry on Wednesday warned that the actions "threaten regional security, undermine freedom of navigation, challenge the rules-based maritime order and jeopardize uninterrupted flow of global commerce."

The Reuters news agency cited an advisory from the European Union's Aspides naval mission in the Red Sea as saying that ships with links to Israel, the United ​States or Saudi Arabia ‌were at a higher risk of being attacked by the Houthis and were advised to avoid voyages through the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden until the threat level decreases.

World.title: US and Saudi Arabia reach historic nuclear energy deal
World.content:
The deal is another sign of growing US-Saudi ties during US President Donald Trump's second term. The agreement, known as a 123 Agreement, would allow Saudi Arabia to build nuclear reactors using US technology.

The United States said on Wednesday it had signed a civilian nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, alongside a separate bilateral safeguards pact.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed the agreements with Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman.

The US Energy Department said the agreements would deepen cooperation between Washington and Riyadh in the civilian nuclear energy sector.

“Together, these two agreements lay the legal foundation for a decadeslong, multi-billion-dollar partnership that advances several priority economic and strategic objectives, including nuclear nonproliferation,” the US Energy Department said in a statement.

Deal allows nuclear reactors and uranium enrichment

The agreement, known as a 123 Agreement, would allow Saudi Arabia to build nuclear reactors using US technology.

It would also permit the Kingdom to enrich uranium and reprocess nuclear waste, activities that can potentially produce material for nuclear weapons.

However, like all signatories to the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, Saudi Arabia has already committed to not developing an atomic bomb and consented ‌to international inspections.

The deal, however, does not include an Additional Protocol that would allow the UN nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, to conduct more intrusive inspections at short notice.

The US administration said the agreement complied with non-proliferation requirements under the Atomic Energy Act.

Washington and Riyadh have discussed nuclear cooperation for years, with Saudi Arabia seeking access to US technology and American companies competing for major contracts.

Why Saudi Arabia is redrawing its global alliances To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What happens next?

The agreement will now be submitted to Congress and will take effect unless lawmakers vote to block it within 90 legislative days.

A two-thirds majority would be required to override a presidential veto.

Several Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns that the agreement could increase proliferation risks and trigger a regional arms race.

“They are allowing Saudi Arabia, a belligerent and authoritarian nation, to develop nuclear weapons technologies while starting a war with Iran under the guise of preventing an Iranian nuclear bomb,” Democratic Senator Edward Markey told Reuters.

“This deal would make us all less safe,” he added.

“This agreement will set off a nuclear race in the region, further disincentivizing Iran from limiting its own program,” Democratic Senator Chris Murphy said on X.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has previously said the kingdom does not want to develop a nuclear weapon but would do so if Iran acquired one.

Saudi Arabia wants nuclear energy to reduce domestic oil use, leaving more crude available for the energy-rich Kingdom to export. Harnassing nuclear power would help Saudi Arabia slash emissions and generate power for energy-intensive services such as desalination and air conditioning.

World.title: US judge sets Maduro trial date for June 2027
World.content:
US prosecutors accuse Maduro of using the power of the Venezuelan state to protect and promote illegal drug smuggling.

A US judge on Wednesday set a date for Venezuelan former President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, to go on trial in New York, where they will face charges of drug trafficking.

The two have been detained since early January, when US forces entered Venezuela and seized them from their Caracas home.

The unprecedented middle-of-the-night raid was hailed by US President Donald Trump as a "surgical law enforcement operation" in a criminal case, which had been brought against the couple six years ago.

Maduro has maintained his innocence, calling himself a prisoner of war and referring to his capture as a kidnapping.

Judge Alvin Hellerstein set June 1, 2027, as the trial date for Maduro and his wife, following a joint request from prosecutors and defense counsel.

Hellerstein also scheduled an upcoming hearing for November 17 to discuss defense motions, including a challenge to the legality of how Maduro and Flores were captured and brought to the United States.

"The ‌parties all ​agree that this is a realistic schedule. We don't think it's going to slip, but obviously if anything comes up we will inform your honor," Maduro's lawyer Barry Pollack told the judge on Wednesday.

Venezuelans want elections — but when will they get them? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Maduro faces life in prison

US prosecutors have accused Maduro of using the power of the Venezuelan state to protect and promote illegal drug smuggling. He has also been accused of forming alliances with cartels to bring tons of cocaine into the United States.

If found guilty, Maduro and Flores face potential life prison sentences.

The pair sat through the 15-minute hearing separately at a defense table, surrounded by their lawyers. They did not speak during the proceedings. But Maduro waved to an unknown person in the courtroom's gallery as he was led out of the courtroom by authorities.

Pollack said his team plans to challenge the indictment on sovereign immunity grounds, saying that if successful, Maduro won't have to continue litigating the case.

Since Maduro was removed from power, Venezuela has been led by his former Vice President Delcy Rodriguez.

Rodriguez reestablished bilateral relationships with the US, with Washington effectively taking over control of Venezuela's oil exports.

In turn, the US has eased sanctions on the country's oil industry, while foreign companies have expanded oil and gas projects.

World.title: Hungary: Ex-PM Orban pledges resistance to Magyar 'tyranny'
World.content:
Hungary's former prime minister alleges that his successor has "dismantled the rule of law and eliminated checks and balances." Peter Magyar has pursued Viktor Orban and his allies since winning April's elections.

Hungary's former Prime Minsiter Viktor Orban accused prosecutors and the new government of sham investigations into his Fidesz party on Wednesday, a day after investigators seized equipment from the party HQ in Budapest as part of a corruption probe.

Hungary's longstanding leader, Orban lost April's general elections in a landslide to conservative rival Peter Magyar, himself a former Fidesz member, in a result hailed by much of Europe but not by the Trump White House.

Since coming to power, Magyar has moved to dismantle what he alleges to be systemic corruption of the Orban and Fidesz era, making a host of sweeping changes. Orban, however, on Wednesday, called these measures signs of "tyranny" and said that he and his opposition party would offer "resistance" by all peaceful means.

Orban chose to appear outside Fidesz's HQ a day after the buidling featured in domestic headlines for other reasons Image: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

What did Orban say?

Orban's online statement late on Tuesday night, followed by his press conference outside the Fidesz HQ on Wednesday, constituted two of his strongest political statements since returning to a role as leader of the opposition in early May after 16 years in power.

On Facebook, he first issued what he called a "statement of resistance" soon after his party announced that prosecutors had searched the party's HQ and seized computer servers and other materials. This is part of a corruption probe into the country's National Culture Fund, which is alleged to have been a state-run payment center for Orban's inner circle and a shadow election campaign fund.

"The National Culture Fund issue was just a pretext for this [search of the party headquarters]," Orban alleged, denying that there had been any wrongdoing.

He said Hungary had "ceased to be a democratic state" after the new center-right government used its parliamentary supermajority to pass a constitutional amendment ending the mandates of the president and the head of the Constitutional Court — both deemed to be Orban allies. He said he and his party would "employ all peaceful means" to oppose an "illegitimate" political system.

On Wednesday, outside Fidesz's base of operations, Orban said he believed Magyar was trying to hobble his party once and for all.

"By yesterday, I had come to realize what this was all about," he told reporters. "What happened was that this served as a pretext to seize Fidesz's servers ... This is a politically motivated legal proceeding designed to render Fidesz — which has clearly survived even this heavy political defeat and is growing stronger — legally unviable."

New laws on term limits mean Orban will not be eligible to stand in Hungary's next elections, assuming they hold Image: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

How and when did Magyar win power?

Peter Magyar's new party, Tisza, comfortably won general elections on April 12, claiming more than 55% of the vote against Fidesz's tally of almost 37%.

Because of Hungary's first-past-the-post electoral system, Magyar now enjoys the same supermajority that Orban often did in his pomp, holding 141 of 199 seats despite having only won 55% of the votes. Fidesz holds just 52 seats.

In Hungary, a two-thirds vote in parliament is needed to amend the constitution.

The new prime minister, who had broken away from Fidesz in 2024, lamenting double standards and institutional corruption, took office on May 9. He had pledged rapid reforms if victorious, but the speed and scope of his actions even took some of his supporters by surprise.

Can the 'dancing minister' fix Hungary's healthcare? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What has Magyar done since taking office to Orban and Fidesz's detriment?

As well as taking steps in foreign policy like trying to mend ties with Brussels and free up assistance for Ukraine since taking office, Magyar has moved quickly against alleged Orban-era corruption and misdeeds. Magyar often refers to this as targeting Orban's "mafia."

Magyar opened up former government facilities to the public to showcase some of the opulence he says indicates systemic corruption.

The national public broadcaster M1, which Tisza and others in opposition said had morphed into Fidesz's mouthpiece, was briefly taken off air this month and broadcast a black full-screen apology to launch a reform process.

Several political appointees have been removed from their roles — most notably President Tamas Sulyok via a constitutional amendment and Constitutional Court president Peter Polt. Magyar this week suggested chess star Judith Polgar for the largely ceremonial role as president, only for her to indicate that she was flattered but not interested.

On Tuesday, Prosecutor General Gabor Balint Nagy, appointed only last year, agreed to step down after being called Orban's "puppet" by Magyar.

Tisza has also introduced term limits of 12 years for all lawmakers, including the prime minister and government ministers. Orban says this means most of the veterans in his party, himself included, will be excluded from the next elections.

He told reporters in Budapest on Wednesday that this harkened back to the late 1980s and the latter days of Communist dictatorship "when there was no democracy in Hungary, there was no rule of law."

Corruption investigations, including but not limited to the investigation into the National Culture Fund, have also struck Orban and his allies.

Some other senior Fidesz members have voluntarily stepped out of the political limelight. Last week, parliamentary caucus leader Gergely Gulyas stepped down, while Orban's longstanding former Foreign Minister Peter Szijjarto left to take up an executive position with Chinese electric carmaker BYD.

Surveys suggest that Orban's party has suffered even more in its first few months in opposition, with one poll by Median this week showing 60% support for Tisza and only 18% for Fidesz.

World.title: Louvre's Apollo Gallery reopens, 9 months after heist
World.content:
The 17th-century Apollo Gallery reopened to the public without precious jewels or other objects previously on display.

Paris' Louvre Museum reopened its Apollo Gallery to the public on Wednesday, marking the first time visitors were allowed in since Ocotber 2025, when robbers stole €88 million ($102 million) worth of crown jewels in a dramatic daytime heist.

The Louvre is world's most visited museum, with guest numbers of up to 9 million a year.

It was originally a royal palace, which was opened to the public during the French Revolution. The museum houses the Mona Lisa, one of the world's most famous pieces of art.

The October 2025 heist shocked the world as the thieves used a crane mounted on a truck to enter the museum through a window at 9:30 a.m., when the museum was still opening.

The group broke in through the window, equipped with power tools like a disc cutter, and stole French crown jewels.

Thieves intended to take a crown, but they dropped it Image: Thomas Clot/MUSEE DU LOUVRE/AFP

Precious jewels relocated

On their way out, the thieves dropped a 170-year-old crown commissioned by Napoleon III as part of a pair of crowns for him and his wife, Empress Eugenie.

The crown was left "badly deformed," the Louvre said, but it was nevertheless "nearly intact" and could be restored. The crown was among other objects that were not taken from the gallery.

Museum operators said the Apollo Gallery will return to its 17th-century original ceremonial purpose, without any of the precious jewels or other objects on display.

The public will be able to tour the majestic room and view its gilded ceilings and Greek frescoes.

The Louvre's director, Christophe Leribault, said the former exhibits have been relocated elsewhere in the museum.

"It's also an opportunity to rediscover the splendid architecture and decor of this gallery," Leribault said.

The Apollo Gallery is considered one of the most marvelous areas of the Louvre, with ceilings designed by Charles Le Brun and later added to by, among others, French painter Eugene Delacroix.

A 'trauma for the entire world'

Leribault took over from former director Laurence des Cars, who resigned in the aftermath of the heist, which highlighted a string of security failures within the museum.

French Culture Minister Catherine Pegard referred to the heist as a "sinister day," adding that it cannot be forgotten.

"It was a trauma for the entire world, which, for several days, expressed its shock and sadness in every language. It was a trauma for us, discovering the fragility of a place we thought unshakeable, and which, like so many others, proved vulnerable," Pegard said.

Authorities have boosted security at the museum, having added new surveillance cameras and anti-intrusion systems.

Security improvements are part of the museum's decade-long modernization plan, estimated to cost up to €800 million.

World.title: Who could be the next UN Secretary-General?
World.content:
For the first time in a decade, the United Nations will soon choose a new Secretary-General. DW takes a look at the six candidates, what they stand for and the challenges they and the UN will face.

After a decade in power, Antonio Guterres, will end his second term as UN Secretary-General on December 31. There are currently six candidates lining up to replace him. Whoever emerges victorious has a tough task, with the relevance, power and financial capability of the UN under an increasingly harsh spotlight.

The UN Secretary-General is "equal parts diplomat and advocate, civil servant and CEO," according to the organization itself. The holder of the position oversees several vital UN organs, including the Security Council, charged with maintaining peace and security.

The 80-year-old UN is struggling for relevance — here's why To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The winning candidate will be selected by the UN's General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council (whose permanent members are China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States), making the path to victory narrow and fraught.

Here's what you need to know about each candidate ahead of a debate between them on Thursday (July 23) at the UN's General Assembly Hall in New York.

Michelle Bachelet

Michelle Bachelet is looking to add another first to her CV Image: Valentin Flauraud/Keystone/picture alliance

The first female president of Chile (from 2006 to 2010 and then 2014 to 2018) is vying to become the first female UN Secretary-General, after several women lost out to Guterres in 2016. "If I am polite, I would say the world was not prepared for it. Is it prepared now? I hope so," Bachelet, 74, said earlier this year. "It will be a very good signal," she said, adding that it would provide hope for many people.

Bachelet also served as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights between 2018 and 2022, a position which saw her involved in many of the key geopolitical issues she would face if elected. While she has admitted she has no "magic formula" to resolve the issues on the Security Council, Bachelet has sought to talk up her experience as a key asset.

Rafael Mariano Grossi

Rafael Grossi is looking to his experience in the nuclear energy sector to boost his bid Image: Efrem Lukatsky/AP Photo/picture alliance

The Argentine diplomat has spent most of his career in the nuclear and atomic energy sectors, culminating in his 2019 appointment as director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), an autonomous organization within the UN.

Given the geopolitical landscape, with nuclear war perceived as an increasing threat, Grossi sees his background as "clearly an advantage. You have to understand the world you live in," he told Swiss outlet Geneva Solutions.

Grossi supports the UN's current attempt at reform known as UN80 and says there is "no need to reinvent the wheel" but wants to streamline the organization with mergers of UN entities and reductions in "duplications, triplications, even quadruplications or quintuplications of structures," which add significant costs to members.

Maria Fernanda Espinosa

Maria Fernanda Espinosa has enjoyed a varied career to date Image: Cyril Zingaro/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

The Spanish-born Ecuadorian has packed plenty into her 61 years. As well as a stint as Ecuador's foreign minister, Espinosa is a poet, essayist and an expert on sustainable development and climate change, particularly in the Amazon region, where she worked with indigenous communities at the beginning of her career.

Espinosa acknowledged the UN's budget difficulties in an interview with UK newspaper The Observer. "The biggest challenge right now is the financial challenge," said Espinosa, who was also president of the UN General Assembly. As a result, she says, the UN must "reform, transform or die."

To achieve such reform, Espinosa wants to work more collaboratively with regional organizations, and lean on Europe, both in financial terms and as a "bridge-builder" between states with conflicting interests and desires.

Rebeca Grynspan

Rebeca Grynspan wants to see the UN be stronger in its approach to problems Image: Cristina Matuozzi/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Vice President of her native Costa Rica between 1994 and 1998, Grynspan is currently Secretary-General of the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), which advocates for developing countries in trade deals. Her work on negotiating a deal between the warring parties for the continued export of Ukrainian grain after the Russian invasion in 2022 has been widely praised.

Grynspan wants the UN to be bolder. "Bureaucracies are very risk-averse by nature, and you cannot have a good idea or take risk," she said at a recent event hosted by think tank Chatham House in London. She has also called for wider representation on the Security Council, particularly from Africa or Latin America.

Macky Sall

A recent return to Senegal seems to have helped Macky Sall get the government behind his candidacy Image: Patrick Meinhardt/AFP

While other candidates have held prominent political positions, Sall's experience is the most recent. The 64-year-old was president of Senegal from 2012 to 2024, having previously served as the country's prime minister.

During his presidential tenure, Senegal saw significant infrastructure improvements. But Sall's popularity took a downward turn in 2021, during his second term, after protests against the imprisonment of opposition leader, Ousmane Sonko. Sall's unsuccessful attempt to postpone the 2024 presidential election, which triggered further deadly protests, has left him a divisive figure in his homeland.

Senegal's current government did not initially support Sarr's candidacy for the UN role but u-turned last month to back his bid.

Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett

Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett has the backing of her native Guyana Image: Bianca Otero/ZUMA/picture alliance

The final candidate to throw their hat in the ring, Rodrigues Birkett entered the race in mid-June. She is the permanent representative of Guyana to the United Nations and has previously undertaken roles in both the UN and as Guyana's foreign minister, Rodrigues Birkett is an Amerindian (the Indigenous peoples of the Americas) and has also held governmental roles related to that community.

Guyana's president Irfaan Ali recently spelt out her UN ambitions.

"Ambassador Rodrigues Burkett's vision for the United Nations centers on strengthening multilateralism, enhancing effectiveness and responsiveness of the organization, promoting inclusive global governance and ensuring the United Nations remains capable of addressing contemporary challenges," he said.

Edited by: Rob Mudge

World.title: How Russia is luring foreign nationals to fight in Ukraine
World.content:
More and more, Russia is recruiting men from the world’s poorest countries to send them to the front in the Ukraine war. Why are people joining up?

Charles Mutoka, a 72-year-old Kenyanis in mourning for his son, Oscar Khagola Mutoka, a former soldier who traveled to Russia in the summer of 2025 to look for work.

His father said that he had tried in vain to talk him out of it. Oscar did not tell him and the rest of his family exactly where he was going but a week after leaving he sent a picture of himself in uniform and never got back in touch again.

His family found out that he had died some time later but, despite appeals to the Kenyan authorities, they were not able to recover the body.

In May 2026, the family held a symbolic memorial service and set up a makeshift burial site for Oscar, in order to at least have a place where they could pray. "The worst part is that I don't know if and where he was actually buried, or if his body was simply dumped in a forest in Russia," Charles Mutoka said.

Charles Mutoka, father of Oscar Khagola Mutoka, a former Kenyan soldier who died fighting in the Ukraine war Image: DW

Oscar Mutoka is one of an estimated 27,000 or more foreign nationals recruited by Russia for its war in Ukraine,according to the Defense Intelligence ofUkraine (HUR). A joint study conducted by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), the Truth Houndshuman rights organization and the Kazakhstan International Bureau for Human Rights and Rule of Law (KIBHR) provides evidence that Russia has set up a global network for recruiting foreign nationals.

"This recruitment targets people in economically, socially and legally precarious life situations. The methods employed range from enticing offers to deception and even coercion," Ilya Nusov, one of the authors of the study, told DW.

'I don't want to starve to death in Cuba'

For many people living in the world's poorest regions, the wages offered by the Russian army is a huge incentive as it means a chance to escape poverty and support their families. That's exactly why Yoan Viondi Mendoza, a Cuban national, decided to work in Russia. He was promised $2,000 (€1,750) per month, an enormous sum by Cuban standards, where the average wage is $20 (€17,50).

DW found out about Yoan Mendoza's story from his brother Michael Duro, who lives in the US. Yoan had wanted to emigrate to the US and be reunited with his brother, but this turned out to be impossible, because of financial and bureaucratic hurdles.

Then he came across a job offer in Russia, his brother said. "Yoan called and said he'd found a way out. He told me about a 'project' in Russia," said Duro, who told DW that he had tried in vain to change his brother's mind.

In September 2023, the Reuters news agency filmed young Cubans who wanted to go to Russia, including Yoan Mendoza who was 23 at the time. He told journalists that he knew exactly where he was going and that he did not want to starve to death in Cuba. He also showed a document that was purportedly a contract with the Russian army, which would also give him Russian citizenship.

Yoan Viondi Mendoza, a Cuban soldier who went to fight for Russia in Ukraine Image: Privat

Duro said that his brother was sent to the front in Ukraine and then tried to escape. "He pleaded, 'I made a mistake. Forgive me. Please get me out of here quickly,'" Diro said, adding that afterwards there was no contact. Yoan's name later surfaced on the lists of foreign nationals killed in action that were published by Ukraine.

'They used us as human shields'

Though Mendoza and Oscar Mutoka probably knew that they were going to Russia to fight in the Ukraine war, many other foreign nationals are being deceived to the front after being promised jobs in construction, security, logistics or agriculture.

That's what happened to Arman Mondol from Bangladesh. He wanted to work abroad to lift his family out of poverty. His father, a farmer, sold some property and took out a loan to pay a recruiter. Mondol was told that he would be working as a packer in a warehouse. Equipped with a tourist visa, he traveled via Saudi Arabia to Russia, where he was then forced to sign a contract in Russian, which he could not read.

Mondol said that he and other foreign nationals had been treated badly in the Russian army. "When we were on a mission, they always sent us ahead while they remained behind us. They used us as human shields and pushed us into the thick of the fighting," he told DW.

Arman Mondol, a Bangladeshi national who was forced into fighting in Russia's war in Ukraine but survived and came home Image: DW

During one of those missions, his vehicle hit a landmine. He was one of only two survivors and was taken to a military hospital, from where he managed to escape. In the end , the Bangladeshi embassy in Moscow helped him to return home, but the war continues to haunt him.

"I still have these images in my mind — dying people, their eyes, their disfigured faces. How they get blown up by landmines. How there was one drone attack after the next. How people's limbs were torn off. It was horrible," Mondol, who still has shrapnel in one leg and has a heavy limp, recalled. Back in his village, he has not found work.

Mercenaries or human trafficking?

Foreign nationals fighting for Russia in Ukraine are often called mercenaries. However, Ilya Nusov explained that, strictly speaking, this isn't what they are according to international law, since often people adopt Russian citizenship before joining the army.

While others had no intention of fighting in the first place. They could be considered the victims of human trafficking, if they are recruited on false premises and coerced. This violates the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, and the Palermo Protocol, which bans human trafficking and has been ratified by most countries in the world, including Russia.

Lured into war: Russia's foreign fighters in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia has insisted that all foreign nationals partaking in the "special military operation," as it calls its war in Ukraine, are involved on a voluntary basis. In March, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov claimed during a press conference with his Kenyan counterpart that "no one is being hired, just as no one is being recruited in the case of the special military operation. Volunteers get there in full compliance with Russian legislation."

DW asked the Russian Foreign Ministry for a statement but had not received a response by the time of publication.

Increasing number of recruited foreign nationals

The involvement of foreign nationals in the war is receiving increased attention, with their families protesting from Nepal to Peru. Some politicians, including Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, have even brought up the subject in meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin. According to media reports, Russia restricted the recruitment of citizens from various "friendly" countries in February 2026. A list of those countries has not been published.

"In some cases, this has contributed to reducing or even stopping the influx of fighters from certain countries at least temporarily," said Nusov. "But we believe that Russia also has ways to circumvent this by reducing recruitment in one place and focusing on a different country." According to Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, Russia could recruit up to 18,500 foreign nationals in 2026.

Benjamin Alvarez Gruber, Nahid Anjuman, Felix Maringa contributed to this article, which was originally published in Russian.

World.title: Si decido comprar una vivienda anunciada por una agencia, ¿estoy obligado a pagar una comisión?
World.content:
Pregunta. ¿En qué supuestos existe obligación de pagar comisión por parte del comprador a la agencia inmobiliaria cuando quien contrata sus servicios es el vendedor? J. Ibáñez

Respuesta. En relación con la obligación de abonar los honorarios de la agencia inmobiliaria por parte del comprador, debe partirse del principio de libertad de pacto entre las partes. En las operaciones de compraventa inmobiliaria no existe una norma que imponga de forma general que la comisión de la agencia deba ser asumida necesariamente por el vendedor o por el comprador, ni de forma exclusiva por uno de ellos, por lo que la dependerá de los acuerdos alcanzados entre las partes.

La parte compradora estará obligada al pago de dichos honorarios cuando haya aceptado de forma clara y expresa asumir ese coste. En la práctica, es habitual que las agencias inmobiliarias incluyan esta cláusula en el parte de visitas, documento que se suele entregar al potencial comprador en la primera visita al inmueble y en el que, además de dejar constancia de que ha conocido la vivienda a través de la agencia, se puede incorporar una cláusula relativa al pago de los honorarios profesionales.

Si dicho parte de visitas contiene una cláusula clara sobre la obligación del comprador de abonar la comisión inmobiliaria, y esta ha sido firmada por la parte compradora, podrá entenderse que existe aceptación contractual suficiente para reclamar el pago de la comisión, siempre que la inmobiliaria haya intervenido efectivamente en la operación y la compraventa llegue finalmente a formalizarse.

Por lo tanto, en el caso que se expone habrá que revisar el documento firmado por el comprador, ya sea el parte de visitas, el documento de entrega de señal o el contrato de arras que habitualmente se suscribe antes de la compraventa. Si en cualquiera de dichos documentos consta expresamente la aceptación del pago de honorarios a favor de la inmobiliaria, sí podrá exigirse el abono de la comisión a la parte compradora. La ley únicamente establece la obligación de pago de los gastos de gestión inmobiliaria al propietario en los supuestos de arrendamiento de vivienda habitual, pero no en las operaciones de compraventa.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Carla Serrano (@la.inercia): “Tengo una lucha encarnizada contra el elitismo cultural”
World.content:
Carla Serrano, o @la.inercia, posa para ICON Design. Ismael Nasrollah

“¡Cotiza!”. Esa es la exhortación que Carla Serrano (Ribeira, 1994) reconoce que le hace “prender” cuando se cuela entre los comentarios de sus redes. “Amor: trabajo en una agencia de marketing digital, me levanto a las 5 de la mañana y tras ocho horas de oficina, me dedico a esto. ¡Tengo dos trabajos!”. Con más de 500.000 seguidores en Instagram gracias a sus videos en los que habla “muy rápido” (su gran coletilla) de historia del arte, cine y cultura, forma parte del creciente número de figuras 3.0 que convierten la cercanía y el dinamismo del mundo online en sus aliados para difundir conocimiento a una audiencia que ha encontrado en las redes una academia virtual.

“Creo que la gente ve contenido de tintes científicos, históricos o culturales y se alegra al pensar que está aprendiendo algo. Pero el hecho de que consumas un contenido cultural no te exime de que quieras luego consumir otro tipo de contenido. Tengo una lucha encarnizada con el elitismo cultural. Sin ir más lejos, hice un contenido comparando a Montoya, de La Isla de las Tentaciones, con un cuadro barroco porque creo que todo está relacionado. La gente agradece la sensación de que no ha perdido el tiempo”, asegura.

Aquí no solo hay una lucha contra el elitismo, sino contra las manecillas del reloj, como demuestran sus redes y su libro, Una historia del arte MUY RÁPIDA: Del Paleolítico al posmodernismo: arte y artistas desde una mirada alternativa (Somos B, 2025). Aunque esa velocidad ha hecho de su perfil un referente para quienes quieren consumir cultura en clave exprés, reconoce que a veces, la fórmula conduce a tropiezos. “En ocasiones, por intentar condensar, falto a la verdad. Ahí entono siempre el mea culpa. No pretendo que la gente se tome los vídeos como una clase magistral, sino que sirvan para despertar curiosidad y que después, cada uno profundice en ella. Quiero que la gente aprenda de sí misma y de la curiosidad”, asegura.

Su referente es Ter, una arquitecta fan de Kim Kardashian que en su canal de YouTube se enfrentó al esnobismo cultural relacionando la arquitectura con la cultura pop. Precisamente Serrano hizo un interesantísimo vídeo en el que explicaba cómo en su paso por la gala MET 2018, al posar Kardashian junto a un sarcófago del sacerdote Nedjemankh luciendo un dorado vestido de Versace, destapó una insólita trama. La pieza había sido saqueada durante la revolución egipcia de 2011 y uno de los saqueadores, al haberse viralizado la imagen, contó lo ocurrido y el fiscal Matthew Bogdanos descubrió que la pieza había sido vendida ilegalmente al MET con documentación falsa. “Es fascinante y refleja cómo la serendipia actúa en la historia del arte”, dice con emoción.

Al hablar con un cómico, la pregunta de cuáles son los límites del humor es tan cansina como necesaria. Ocurre lo mismo en la actualidad cuando se plantea si es posible separar la obra del artista al conversar sobre arte. “Creo que prácticamente todos los historiadores del arte mantenemos la postura de que hacerlo es complicado. El punto de vista adecuado es el self-awareness”, asegura. Y si de algo es ella consciente es de su propio privilegio.

“Tenemos un sesgo cultural inmenso del que hemos de ir siendo conscientes. Muchas veces, reviso mis últimos reels y me doy cuenta de que llevo muchísimos vídeos hablando de Estados Unidos y decido cambiar las cosas. Soy una mujer europea y por lo tanto, tengo que romper ese privilegio y esa perspectiva”, dice. En su libro se esfuerza también por reivindicar a esas pintoras y fotógrafas olvidadas, algo que a algunos les molesta. “Si quiero poner en valor la figura de Artemisia Gentileschi, no quiero decir que Caravaggio no fuese importante. Negar que el arte, el cine y la historia han hecho un borrado de las mujeres es negar la realidad. ¡No queremos borrar a los hombres ni hacer un borrado de historia! No hay que molestarse y quien lo haga, tiene que revisarse”. Y punto.

World.title: Ivory and a rhino skull among 5,800 items handed to RVO
World.content:
Some 5,800 prohibited objects including elephant ivory have been anonymously handed in to the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO) over the past year, a more than fivefold increase on the previous year.

“Never before has so much been handed in,” says The Hague-based RVO, including “moving boxes with a thousand [pieces of] ivory jewellery, a rhino skull with a gunshot wound, crocodile leather bags, musical instruments and an elephant’s leg.”

The objects also included taxidermy animals such as a long-eared owl, peregrine falcon and turtles. Pictures on broadcaster NOS show ivory binoculars and crocodile leather bags.

The sale and trade of elephant ivory are strictly regulated under European CITES laws (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species), with permits required for the possession and trade of protected plants or animals.

Most of the items, which can be handed in at a drop-off bin in The Hague or even by post, are destroyed to prevent them from (re)entering the illegal trade. The RVO says it uses a small number of the items for research and education.

World.title: Thuisbezorgd hides costs and fakes discounts: consumer group
World.content:
The food delivery platform Thuisbezorgd.nl hides compulsory charges and advertises fake discounts, the Dutch consumer association Consumentenbond said on Tuesday, calling on the company to stop and to compensate affected customers.

Mandatory costs should be clearly shown before a customer starts ordering, the association said, but Thuisbezorgd’s app and website do not reveal compulsory “service” charges – for items such as bags, plastic packaging and sauce – until part-way through or at the end of an order, adding an average of €2 to €4 to the bill.

The association also said the company broke rules on special offers. Under Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM) rules, a struck-through sale price must be the lowest the seller charged in the previous 30 days. In one case, the association found Indian snacks that had previously cost €3.75 being offered “on sale” from €7.50 to €6.

“We have been in talks with Thuisbezorgd since March, but the platform is still confronting customers with hidden costs and fake discounts,” said Consumentenbond director Sandra Molenaar, noting the company has more than six million users in the Netherlands.

Because the practice has probably been going on for years, the association estimates the hidden costs run into the hundreds of millions of euros in total. A Thuisbezorgd spokesperson said the company did not recognise the association’s accusations.

The Consumentenbond said it had also found hidden costs at Uber Eats, which made changes in June, though no fake discounts. The findings are part of a wider campaign against hidden charges and misleading offers that also named Bol and Amazon last week.

The association can press companies to change but cannot impose penalties; that is a matter for the ACM, which has fined firms including Leen Bakker, G-Star and Jysk in the past.

World.title: Three arrested over €5m smartphone heist near Schiphol
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Three men have been arrested over the theft of a shipment of smartphones with an estimated street value of around €5 million from the Schiphol area, the Royal Military Police (Koninklijke Marechaussee) have said.

The suspects are two 24-year-old men from Amsterdam and a 39-year-old from Zoetermeer.

The shipment went missing on June 18, prompting an investigation, led by the Noord-Holland public prosecution department, into an organised crime group.

One of the suspects works for a transport company at Schiphol and is thought to have passed confidential information to the group, the military police said. Further arrests have not been ruled out.

World.title: Two trams collide on Rotterdam’s Erasmus Bridge, 15 injured
World.content:
Fifteen people were injured, one of them seriously, when two trams collided on the Erasmus Bridge in Rotterdam on Wednesday morning, the regional safety board has said. One of the trams was derailed by the impact.

The crash happened at around 11.10am, regional broadcaster Rijnmond reported. Footage shows one tram coming to a halt as it drove onto the bridge from the direction of the city centre, before a second tram approached from behind and ran into it, apparently without braking.

The seriously injured person was trapped and had to be freed before being taken to hospital. The safety board initially reported 18 injured and two seriously hurt, but later revised the figures.

Transport company RET said it could not yet say what caused the rear-end collision, adding that it was shocked by the footage and that its thoughts were with the victims and passengers. Two cars were also damaged, the fire service said.

The power to the overhead lines was switched off and the bridge closed to traffic, halting tram services on lines 3 and 5.

World.title: Man jailed for 15 months over threats to Groningen butchers
World.content:
A Groningen court has sentenced a 23-year-old man to 15 months in prison for sending death threats to butchers in the province and neighbouring Drenthe.

Prosecutors requested a four-year sentence, saying he had a terrorist motive. But the court ruled there was insufficient evidence for such a charge, saying instead he acted out of radical environmental and animal-rights beliefs.

Because four months of his sentence are suspended, the man, known as Bas V., will be released immediately, having already served his time in pre-trial detention. He is bound by a three-year probationary period.

The crime

Last September, Bas V. sent threatening emails to 12 butcher shops demanding they close. “You get one warning, nothing more. If the shop isn’t closed tomorrow, I will come with a machete and stab everyone to death,” read the email.

The court stated: “The texts on his phone say something about his mindset, but not that he wanted to disrupt society with them.”

Bas V., who admitted to sending the emails, was arrested after seven of the butchers filed a complaint. Police found a machete in his home and notes on his phone saying he also needed a pistol with a silencer to “kill people responsible for the humiliation of animals,” according to broadcaster NOS.

The national broadcaster also says that Bas V. was found by experts to have a gaming addiction, a cannabis addiction, ADHD and autism, and will be placed in a protected living facility to receive treatment.

World.title: House prices rising fastest in Groningen, slowest in Amsterdam

House prices are climbing fastest in Groningen and slowest in the Randstad, figures from the national statistics office CBS and the Land Registry showed on Tuesday.

Homes in Groningen province cost 7.9% more in the second quarter than a year earlier – the biggest rise in the country – while in Noord-Holland prices went up just 2.4%.

House prices rose 4.2% nationwide, the tenth quarter running that they have climbed, though more slowly than the 5.2% jump in the first three months of the year. After Groningen, the steepest rises were in Drenthe, Gelderland and Friesland, all above 5%.

Of the four biggest cities, The Hague rose most, at 4.5%, while Amsterdam barely moved, up 0.8%. Fewer homes sold than a year earlier in both Amsterdam and Rotterdam.

Nearly 59,000 homes changed hands across the country, 2.7% more than the same quarter last year.

As the conflict between the US and Iran escalates, the foreign affairs ministry has tightened its advice for people wanting to travel to the region.

With Iran targeting US allies in the Middle East in response to American attacks, the Dutch government has advised against travelling to Qatar, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates – which includes the popular holiday destination of Dubai – unless absolutely necessary.

That falls under the ministry’s orange travel advisory, which discourages all travel unless there’s an emergency, such as the death of a family member.

The travel advice for Bahrain has moved up to red, meaning the ministry says the Dutch embassy cannot offer help. “Whatever your situation is, don’t travel there,” the ministry said. “It’s too dangerous.”

The US, UK, Canada and Australia have also updated their travel alerts for Gulf countries in recent days.

Check the ministry’s website for the latest travel advisories.

World.title: Explosive attacks fall as task force targets young offenders
World.content:
Attacks using explosives fell by more than 17% in the first half of this year, the first substantial drop since the wave of explosions peaked in 2024, according to the government’s Offensive against Explosions (OTE) working group.

The number of explosions or attempted explosions decreased from 705 during the first half of 2025 to 581 during the same time, putting the OTE on track to achieve a 10% decrease this year.

But explosions remain a serious safety threat – and it’s mostly young people who use them to commit crimes. Almost half of all arrested suspects were minors, reports NU.nl, with fewer than one in six suspects older than 30. A large proportion of offenders are under the age of 25.

“Every attack is one too many,” said Carola Schouten, mayor of Rotterdam and chairwoman of the OTE. “But it is good to see that the number of attacks is starting to decrease nationwide… This requires continued attention and joint commitment on all fronts.”

Young offenders

Specifically, the task force is focusing on reducing the number of young offenders, finding and prosecuting those who hire them and their intermediaries and limiting the availability of explosives – in this case mostly powerful, illegally trafficked fireworks, often procured from neighbouring countries like Germany or ordered online.

“This is done, among other things, by disrupting the production, transport, storage and trade in such explosives,” said the OTE, which is also setting up a joint Europol task force with Germany and Sweden, and lobbying with France and Sweden for tighter EU rules on powerful fireworks.

But given the young age of offenders, prevention is the name of the game. The OTE has begun a pilot focusing on conflict mediation among young people, while parents, caregivers and those who work with them are being given support to make “young people more resilient to (online) temptations to crime”.

While Poland already hosts various allied forces, the presence of German troops is particularly symbolic given the two countries’ difficult history. “United, we will prevail,” wrote the General Staff of the Polish Armed Forces (SGWP), announcing the deployment. “This is what allied cooperation looks like in practice, which translates into greater military readiness and strengthens NATO’s defensive potential.” Polscy i niemieccy żołnierze razem wzmacniają granicę z Rosją. They said that the German personnel would mainly engage in engineering work, such as digging trenches, laying barbed wire and constructing anti-tank barriers. Today, Poland’s SGWP confirmed that “several dozen” German troops, including “highly specialised engineering forces” along with their equipment, had since June been temporarily deployed to “support the Polish armed forces in expanding defence infrastructure on NATO’s northeastern flank”. It emphasised that the East Shield project is “purely defensive in nature” and comes in “response to threats stemming from, among others, Russian aggression against Ukraine”. While the armed forces did not reveal the location of the deployment, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated in a social media post that it was on the Russian border. Poland has a 210-km frontier with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. German public broadcaster Deutsche Welle reports that the activities of the German sappers are focused in particular on improving defences around the so-called Suwałki Gap, a strategically important stretch of land around the Polish-Lithuanian border between Belarus and Kaliningrad. “Together, we are ensuring Europe’s security,” said Lieutenant General Alexander Sollfrank, the Bundeswehr’s operational commander, announcing the deployment today. “Through our engagement in Poland, we are strengthening NATO’s defence capabilities and underscoring the alliance’s unwavering commitment to ensuring peace through unity and credible deterrence.” Poland and Germany have signed a bilateral security agreement that will see the two neighbours and NATO allies increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity https://t.co/6BPX2WxvxH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 17, 2026 SGWP, which shared footage of Polish and German forces installing anti-tank barriers, said the work aims to “hinder and delay an aggressor’s actions in the event of a threat”, thereby “increasing the time for a response from the Polish armed forces and the entire [NATO] alliance”. It also seeks to “create conditions for the efficient reception, deployment and use of NATO forces on Polish territory”. SGWP welcomed “the involvement of the German contingent as a practical expression of allied solidarity and the result of consistently developing military cooperation between Poland and Germany”. It also noted that the cooperation would help the two sides improve their ability to operate jointly, including “developing the competencies necessary for conducting a joint defence operation”. However, it emphasised that the current deployment is focused on training and engineering, with no combat component, and that the German troops are unarmed. SGWP also emphasised that the East Shield operation remains entirely a Polish national programme. Poland’s climate and environment ministry has inaugurated the first of 11 planned “community forests” around large cities, with the aim of giving residents a place for recreation and contact with nature while also helping to fulfil the government’s pledge to reduce logging. Plans for the forests were announced in 2024, and the first has now been established around Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city. Ten other major urban centres, including Warsaw, Kraków, Poznań and Łódź, are set to follow. Dotrzymujemy słowa. Powołaliśmy pierwsze lasy społeczne w Polsce, to lasy ochronne wokół Wrocławia. Kolejne miasta przed nami. @MKiS_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/RxhsMZShj9 — Paulina Hennig-Kloska (@hennigkloska) July 21, 2026 “This is a historic moment and the beginning of a new approach to forest protection – with residents in mind first and foremost,” said climate and environment minister Paulina Hennig-Kloska at an inauguration ceremony outside Wrocław on Sunday. “Community forests are places where residents can relax, play sports and simply spend time close to nature,” she added. “At the same time, they are crucial to our security and quality of life: they retain water, regulate the climate, purify the air and protect the soil.” An area covering 13,000 hectares (32,124 acres) has been designated as a community forest around Wrocław. Forest management there will now be aimed at “maximising the forest’s social functions”, says the ministry, while timber harvesting is also restricted. The area will be divided into three zones, including “natural forests”, where nature will be left to take its course, and “near-natural forests” with minimal intervention. However, the largest zone, amounting to over 8,000 hectares, will be “social forests”, which the state forestry agency says “will be managed in a way that ensures the comfort of those who use the forest and its benefits related to wellbeing, physical exercise and recreation”. Hennig-Kloska noted that, in the latter area, educational trails as well as hiking and cycling paths would be established. However, given that such facilities already exist in many forests, it remains unclear how the new community forests will differ. The ministry is now conducting consultations and analysis on establishing community forests around ten other designated urban centres: Bielsko-Biała, Tricity (Gdańsk-Gdynia-Sopot), Katowice, Kielce, Kraków, Łódź, Poznań, Szczecin, Toruń-Bydgoszcz and Warsaw. On Sunday, Hennig-Kloska said that the “next in line” to have their community forests established are Kielce and Bielsko-Biała, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Shortly after coming to power in December 2023, the current government announced that it would halt planned logging in some forests. The former Law and Justice (PiS) administration had faced criticism for overseeing an increase in logging, especially in Białowieża Forest. The current government also launched plans to create Poland’s first new national parks in over two decades. However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki last year vetoed that move, arguing that it would “block the economic development of the region” and threaten Poland’s security.
