World.title: Russia destroyed 40,000 Armenian roses shipped via Belarus
World.content:
Russia destroys Armenian roses

Officials from Russia‘s agricultural watchdog Rosselkhoznadzor in Smolensk Region discovered a shipment of freshly cut roses from Armenia that was being transported via Belarus.

According to the Belarusian outlet Euroradio, the shipment was deemed illegal because Russia has banned the import of nearly all Armenian goods since the spring.

Armenian roses imported via Belarus / 32.fsvps.gov.ru

Moscow says the import ban was imposed in response to what it described as violations of phytosanitary requirements. However, the restrictions were introduced after Armenia declared EU integration as a foreign policy goal, leading officials in Yerevan and the EU to view the move as politically motivated.

Russia has previously imposed similar trade restrictions on Georgia and Moldova to exert economic pressure amid political disagreements.

According to the accompanying documents, the lorry travelling from Belarus’s Minsk Region to Moscow was carrying non-alcoholic carbonated energy drinks. However, an inspection found 39,200 roses instead.

The flowers were being transported without the required phytosanitary certificates or shipping documents.

Rosselkhoznadzor said some of the boxes still bore labels identifying Armenia as the country of origin.

The roses were destroyed, while the carrier was held administratively liable.

Russia suspends flower imports from Iran over suspected re-exports from Armenia

Shortly after the reports emerged that Armenian roses transported via Belarus had been destroyed, Russia’s agricultural watchdog Rosselkhoznadzor suspended the certification of flowers for export to Russia from Iran, also over suspicions that they had been re-exported from Armenia.

The agency said flower shipments from Iran in 2026 had significantly exceeded the volume recorded during the same period last year.

Rosselkhoznadzor also said that although Iran was listed as the exporting country, the appearance of the flowers and their packaging were identical to products previously supplied from Armenia.

Background

Since early spring 2026, Russia has gradually introduced restrictions on Armenian products.

Initially, the measures targeted Jermuk mineral water, followed by a range of alcoholic beverages.

On 30 May, Russia banned imports from Armenia of tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, herbs and strawberries.

This was followed by a temporary ban imposed by the Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance (Rosselkhoznadzor) on the import of flowers and ornamental plants from Armenia.

Rosselkhoznadzor has also reported problems with imports of certain livestock products, as well as fish and fish products.

Armenia also received a letter from Russia warning of the possible termination of an agreement on supplies of natural gas, petroleum products and rough diamonds.

The restrictions imposed by Russia are significant for Armenia, as the Russian market has been the main destination for Armenian agricultural exports for decades.

The Armenian authorities are currently working, with active support from the European Union, to rapidly open alternative export markets for Armenian products.

World.title: Armenia begins recruiting and training border guards for Azerbaijan border
World.content:
Armenia launches border guard recruitment

The Armenian government plans to gradually transfer responsibility for guarding the entire Armenia-Azerbaijan border from the Defense Ministry to the Border Guard Troops of the National Security Service (NSS).

To make that possible, the agency needs additional personnel. The government therefore plans to expand the NSS by introducing the “I Have the Honor“ programme, which the Defense Ministry already runs successfully.

Under the programme, university students sign a contract to undergo military training while completing their studies. After graduation, they perform their military service at the location and under the conditions specified in the contract.

Under the new proposal, participants will first serve as conscripts in the rank of private in Defense Ministry units. They will then transfer to the NSS as commissioned officers.

“The new mechanism will help strengthen the National Security Service, particularly the Border Guard Troops, by recruiting personnel with higher education,” the explanatory note to the draft says.

Under an intergovernmental agreement signed in 1992, the Russian Federal Security Service’s Border Guard Service has been responsible for guarding Armenia’s borders with Turkey and Iran. In recent years, however, Armenia has steadily moved to place the protection of its borders entirely under its own control. In 2024, Russian border guards withdrew from Zvartnots International Airport and from border areas along the frontier with Azerbaijan. On January 1, 2025, Russian border guards also left the border crossing on the Armenia-Iran frontier. Then, on March 1, Armenia’s National Security Service assumed sole responsibility for guarding the Margara border crossing with Turkey. Since the beginning of 2026, only Armenian border guards have been serving at the Akhurik border crossing on the Armenia-Turkey border.

Deferring military service during university in exchange for serving as an officer

The “I Have the Honor” programme allows students to defer compulsory military service while at university. In return, they commit to serving later as commissioned officers.

“Students attend university free of charge, with the state covering tuition fees in full at the rate set by the university for the relevant programme.”

After graduating from university and completing the required military training, participants receive the rank of lieutenant and begin contract service.

Officers receive their assignments through a lottery system.

Those trained as platoon commanders serve for two years and three months.

Those trained for military medical service serve for four years after graduation, followed by one year of clinical residency.

What other changes does the draft propose?

The legislative package also includes amendments to several laws governing military service, the National Security Service’s Border Guard Troops, and the country’s national security agencies.

In particular, the draft would clearly define the circumstances in which NSS officers may use firearms, special equipment and physical force.

Before using force, officers would have to issue a warning and allow enough time for a person to comply with a lawful order, unless any delay posed an immediate danger. The draft also requires officers to use force proportionately to the level of resistance or threat. They would also have to provide first aid to anyone injured.

If parliament passes the legislative package, border guards will also be able to use video and audio recording devices while carrying out their duties.

The draft would also raise the retirement age for senior NSS officers from 52 to 55.

Armenia launches border guard recruitment

World.title: Georgia’s Asian pivot: What does Tbilisi seek in Central Asia?
World.content:
Georgia’s Asian pivot

A section of Georgia’s Baku–Tbilisi–Kars highway. Photo: Reuters

Since the start of summer 2026, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has met the leaders of all five Central Asian states.

Tbilisi has signed strategic partnership agreements with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. The Georgian prime minister has also made his first official visits to Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. In July, Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov paid his first official visit to Tbilisi.

The Georgian government says the renewed engagement is aimed at strengthening the country’s role as a regional transit hub. For the Central Asian states, new trade routes are becoming increasingly important alongside those through Russia and China.

Georgia is offering them access from the Caspian Sea to the Black Sea and onwards to Europe.

The growing ties with Central Asia come against the backdrop of an almost complete freeze in relations between Tbilisi and the West. The European Union has significantly scaled back political contacts with the Georgian government and suspended part of its direct assistance.

According to official EU statements, the measures are a response to what Brussels describes as democratic backsliding in Georgia.

Georgia’s EU accession process has effectively been put on hold until the government changes its political course. The EU’s 2026 report states that no political dialogue took place between the EU and Georgia during the reporting period.

Against this backdrop, the Georgian government describes its foreign policy as multi-vector.

Central Asia has become one of the main pillars of that policy. The key question, however, is what lies behind this shift: an effort to expand Georgia’s economic opportunities, or a political response to deteriorating relations with the West?

Economic data present a mixed picture. Exports to Central Asia have increased, but most of the growth is not driven by goods produced in Georgia. Re-exported vehicles account for the bulk of exports to Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.

Moreover, Central Asia’s interest in Georgia is largely based on access to Western markets. If Tbilisi moves away from the European political and economic space, its value as a transit hub could also diminish.

Kyrgyzstan: Exports driven almost entirely by vehicle re-exports

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze visited Kyrgyzstan on 11 June 2026. According to the Georgian government, it was the first official meeting between the two countries at the highest level.

Kobakhidze held talks with President Sadyr Japarov. Bishkek also hosted the second meeting of the Georgian-Kyrgyz Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov.

The two sides signed a series of agreements covering aviation, veterinary services, education, sport, legal cooperation and the management of state property. They also signed an agreement on the advance exchange of customs information.

Trade was the main economic focus of the talks. However, Georgia’s exports to the region remain heavily dependent on re-exports.

According to Georgia’s statistics office, Geostat, the country exported goods worth $355.2m to Kyrgyzstan between January and May 2026, while imports amounted to just $1.2m. In 2025, exports reached almost $1.5bn.

Data for the first four months of 2026 show that passenger cars accounted for 95.5% of exports. Other goods made up only a small share and included alcoholic drinks, soft drinks, lorries and medicines.

In practice, however, Kyrgyzstan is only nominally one of Georgia’s largest export markets. Georgia does not manufacture the cars it exports. Instead, it acts as an intermediary, purchasing, servicing and re-exporting the vehicles.

Direct investment from Kyrgyzstan also remains limited. It totalled $374,000 in 2025, down from $656,000 in 2024.

The most significant long-term project is the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, which will connect the Chinese city of Kashgar with Andijan in Uzbekistan via Kyrgyzstan.

Tbilisi expects the railway to bring additional freight to the Middle Corridor. The cargo would then travel through other Central Asian states, across the Caspian Sea, and onwards via Azerbaijan and Georgia.

According to Mariam Kvrivishvili, a significant increase in cargo volumes is expected from around 2031. However, different completion dates have been cited for the railway project, while the onward route across the Caspian Sea has yet to be finalised.

Georgia and Kyrgyzstan are also considering launching direct flights. In 2025, Georgia received 21,542 visitors from Kyrgyzstan. The figure remained virtually unchanged in the first quarter of 2026.

Tajikistan: Relations beginning to take institutional shape

Kobakhidze visited Tajikistan on 19-20 June in what was the first official visit by a senior Georgian official.

The prime minister held talks with President Emomali Rahmon and Prime Minister Kokhir Rasulzoda. During the visit, the two sides signed 11 agreements. Previously, only three bilateral agreements had been in force.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Tajik President Emomali Rahmon.

Tbilisi and Dushanbe established an intergovernmental commission on economic cooperation. Agreements were also signed in the fields of air transport, tourism and agriculture.

The two sides identified a broad range of potential areas for cooperation, including trade, investment, transport, energy and mining. Pharmaceuticals, artificial intelligence and digitalisation were also mentioned.

However, no specific projects in these sectors have yet been announced.

Trade with Tajikistan has also been boosted by vehicle re-exports. In 2025, Georgian exports totalled $179.6m, while imports did not reach even $1m. Between January and May 2026, exports fell to $47m.

In 2025, Georgia exported 7,592 passenger cars to Tajikistan worth $162.3m. They accounted for about 90% of total exports.

Other exports included medicines, soft drinks, mineral water and heavy machinery, but their combined share remained small compared with cars.

Direct investment from Tajikistan in Georgia is virtually non-existent. Tourist flows are also limited. In 2025, Georgia recorded 4,704 visits from Tajikistan, fewer than in 2024.

The two sides also plan to launch direct flights between Tbilisi and Dushanbe. However, no date has yet been announced for the start of services.

Tajikistan is a landlocked country with no direct access to the Middle Corridor. Its cargo must pass through other Central Asian states before reaching the Caspian Sea. As a result, linking Tajikistan to Georgia’s transit route requires coordination among several countries.

Kazakhstan: Georgia’s most viable economic and energy partner

Irakli Kobakhidze visited Kazakhstan on 29 June, where he met President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov.

The main political outcome of the visit was a joint statement on strategic partnership. Tokayev also awarded Kobakhidze the first-class Order of Friendship.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

The economic talks covered the Middle Corridor, energy, the port of Anaklia and tourism.

Of the five Central Asian states, Kazakhstan has the most extensive economic ties with Georgia. However, passenger cars also dominate Georgian exports to the country.

In 2025, Georgian exports to Kazakhstan reached $910m. Between January and May 2026, they fell to $218.2m, while imports over the same period amounted to $34.5m.

The main reason for the decline was a drop in vehicle re-exports. In the first five months of 2026, car exports amounted to $163.8m.

Georgia also exports mineral water, soft drinks, poultry meat and frozen fish to Kazakhstan. In return, it imports oil, petroleum products, wheat, cotton and metal ores.

Oil transit is another important area of cooperation. According to Tokayev, Kazakhstan plans to increase oil shipments through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline.

Transporting Kazakh oil through the pipeline reduces the country’s dependence on Russian routes, while generating additional transit revenue for Georgia.

According to a BP report, 49m barrels of oil were transported through the pipeline in the first quarter of 2026, equivalent to about six million tonnes.

The port of Anaklia is also important for Kazakhstan. According to Georgia’s Economy Ministry, the port project was one of the main topics discussed during the meetings in Astana.

Kazakhstan is Central Asia’s wealthiest country in terms of natural resources. It has reserves of oil, uranium, copper, tungsten and other important minerals. Western interest in the country is therefore linked not only to transport routes.

In November 2025, Kazakhstan signed a $1.1bn agreement with a US company to develop a tungsten deposit. The deal illustrates the scale of Western economic interest in Central Asia.

Uzbekistan: Strategic partnership and interest in Georgian ports

Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev visited Georgia in July 2026. He and Irakli Kobakhidze signed a declaration on strategic partnership.

The two sides also signed agreements covering the economy, finance, customs, education and healthcare. The documents also addressed agriculture, culture and information technology.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev

Following the visit, Uzbekistan’s investment and transport ministers toured the ports of Anaklia and Poti. They also visited the Poti Free Industrial Zone.

Uzbekistan views Georgia as an important partner and transit hub in the South Caucasus. Its main interest lies in trade routes and access to Black Sea ports.

In 2025, Georgian exports to Uzbekistan totalled $220.2m, while imports reached $89.4m. Between January and May 2026, exports amounted to $64.3m and imports to $25.9m.

Investment remains far more limited. Uzbek direct investment in Georgia totalled just $220,000 in 2025. In the first quarter of 2026, it stood at $276,000.

Over the past six years, Georgia has received about $19m in investment from Uzbekistan. Uzbek businesspeople have mainly shown interest in trade, property and the hotel sector.

The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway is also important for Uzbekistan. The project will provide the country with a direct rail link to China. The route could also be extended towards the Caspian Sea and Georgia.

The visits to Georgian ports were a practical sign of this interest. However, no specific Uzbek investments in the ports of Anaklia or Poti have yet been announced.

Turkmenistan: Gas, oil and access to Black Sea

Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov arrived in Georgia on 17 July, where he held talks with President Mikheil Kavelashvili and Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

The main topics of the talks were the Middle Corridor, TRACECA, port infrastructure and energy cooperation. The two sides also signed agreements covering education, industry and healthcare.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov.

The Turkmen president spoke of the joint use of ports on the Caspian and Black seas.

“Serious negotiations are already under way on the use of port infrastructure. This involves using ports on the Caspian and Black seas on a mutually beneficial basis,” Berdimuhamedov said.

He did not name any specific ports or provide details on the scale of investment or the project’s timeline.

In 2025, Georgian exports to Turkmenistan totalled $63.6m, while imports exceeded $39m. Between January and May 2026, bilateral trade fell to about $38.6m.

Georgia mainly imports oil and petroleum products from Turkmenistan, while exporting passenger cars and meat.

Energy expert Murman Margvelashvili sees short-term potential for refining Turkmen oil in Georgia, particularly at the new oil refinery in Kulevi.

A more long-term project is the Trans-Caspian gas pipeline. It would carry Turkmen gas across the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan, before continuing through Georgia and Turkey.

“A more strategic and long-term direction could be a project that has been under discussion for many years: the Trans-Caspian gas pipeline,” Margvelashvili said.

Turkmenistan has some of the world’s largest natural gas reserves. However, the Trans-Caspian pipeline has been discussed for several decades and there is currently no firm timetable for its implementation.

Middle Corridor: shared strategic interest for Georgia and Central Asia

One issue featured consistently in Georgia’s talks with all five Central Asian states: the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, better known as the Middle Corridor.

What is the Middle Corridor? The Middle Corridor, officially known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), is an international trade route linking China and Central Asia with Europe while bypassing Russia. The route runs through China, Kazakhstan, across the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan, through Georgia and onwards across the Black Sea to Europe. Why is it important? nterest in the Middle Corridor has grown since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as European and Asian businesses have sought alternatives to transport routes passing through Russia. The corridor offers several advantages: — it reduces dependence on Russian transit routes; — provides an alternative to the Northern Corridor; — can be faster than maritime shipping in some cases; — and connects Central Asian economies with European markets. Georgia’s role Georgia is one of the key countries along the Middle Corridor: — it provides the rail and road links connecting Azerbaijan with the Black Sea; — it is home to the ports of Poti and Batumi; — the planned deep-water port at Anaklia is widely seen as central to expanding the corridor’s capacity. Its main advantage is that it would be able to accommodate large container ships, something Georgia’s existing ports cannot fully support.

The Middle Corridor has gained strategic importance since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Central Asian countries are seeking alternatives to transporting goods through Russia, while Western governments and businesses are increasingly interested in supply chains that are less dependent on both Russia and China.

However, the Middle Corridor still faces a number of challenges:

Limited capacity at ports on the Caspian and Black seas;

Customs procedures that differ from one country to another;

A lack of coordinated tariff policies;

Delays at the junctions between maritime and rail transport;

High transportation costs;

Insufficient infrastructure.

As a result, political declarations alone will not be enough to make the corridor competitive. It will require ports, railways, a digital customs system and a coordinated tariff policy.

Anaklia: A project that could benefit Central Asia

The Georgian government has described the deep-water port of Anaklia as the key infrastructure project of the Middle Corridor.

According to the Ministry of Economy, the first phase of construction is scheduled for completion in 2029. The port will have an annual capacity of at least 600,000 TEU and will be capable of handling Panamax-class vessels.

The marine works are being carried out by the Belgian company Jan De Nul. However, the port operator has yet to be selected, and the project’s final financing model has not yet been determined.

The issue of Anaklia was discussed separately during meetings with the Kazakh and Uzbek delegations. Experts suggest that companies from Central Asia could eventually be considered as operators of the port’s terminals. The Georgian government has not announced any such agreement.

Anaklia’s commercial success will depend on securing guaranteed cargo volumes. For Georgia, therefore, agreements with Central Asian countries are not merely a matter of diplomacy. They also form part of the port’s economic rationale.

Western interest in Central Asia

Central Asia is not only a priority for the Georgian government. The United States, the European Union, China and Russia are all deepening their engagement with the region.

In April 2025, the EU and the five Central Asian states upgraded their relations to a strategic partnership. The bloc also announced a €12 billion Global Gateway investment package covering transport, critical raw materials, energy, water and digital connectivity.

In June 2026, the European Commission launched a new platform to develop transport infrastructure linking Europe with Central Asia via the Black Sea and the South Caucasus. Agreements signed with international financial institutions are expected to mobilise up to €2 billion in investment.

The United States’ primary interest lies in critical minerals. Central Asia is rich in uranium, copper, tungsten, gold and rare earth elements.

The countries of the region are using this growing interest to balance their foreign policies. They continue to cooperate with Russia and China while also seeking access to Western capital and markets.

What does closer cooperation with Central Asia mean for Georgia?

Experts agree that cooperation with Central Asia is important for Georgia. At the same time, the government is presenting these ties as a possible alternative to the country’s traditional Western orientation.

According to economist Rati Tsiklauri, the economic relationship between Georgia and Central Asia appears more substantial in official statements than it does in the actual trade statistics.

“Ultimately, all cooperation with Central Asia comes down to our role as a transit country. Unfortunately, our economy is not large enough to sustain a fully fledged two-way exchange of goods with these countries,” Tsiklauri said.

In Tsiklauri’s view, closer cooperation with Central Asia is a positive development. However, it should not become compensation for Georgia’s deteriorating relationship with the West.

“We should not try to build ties with East and Central Asia only to present them as proof that we no longer need the West because we have China, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan. That simply won’t work,” Tsiklauri said.

Nika Alavidze, Georgia’s former deputy economy minister and co-founder of the public movement Georgia First, focuses on the quality of trade. In his view, vehicle re-exports generate revenue, but they cannot serve as a sustainable model for economic development.

“Re-exports do not create industry. Growing oil exports do not mean energy independence. Higher trade turnover does not amount to a technological breakthrough,” Alavidze wrote on his blog.

He argues that “portraying Asia as an alternative to the West is a dangerous political illusion.”

“The circumstances created by the Russia-Ukraine war have opened a temporary trade window for Georgia, but that is not a strategy—especially when it comes with serious reputational risks,” Alavidze said.

In his view, Georgia’s greatest asset is its integration with the Western system. The country can become a reliable legal, financial and transit platform for Central Asia, but only if it remains connected to European rules and standards.

“What matters to Central Asian markets is Georgia’s geopolitical role, not simply its geographical location. They fully understand that geography alone offers them nothing. By contrast, Georgia’s geopolitical weight allows them to integrate their economic model, culture, legal framework and institutions more smoothly with major Western markets. Asia needs a connection to Europe, just as Europe needs a connection to Asia. If we limit ourselves to serving only as a geographical corridor, we will gain nothing, remain merely a transit route and ultimately be left with little more than environmental or infrastructure-related costs alongside short-term benefits,” Alavidze said.

Economist Elguja Khokrishvili also sees Georgia’s geographical advantage as only a temporary opportunity. In his view, cargo owners will continue to use the Georgian corridor only as long as it remains competitive.

Khokrishvili also notes that the Central Asian countries possess other sources of leverage. Kazakhstan offers partners oil, uranium and a large market. Uzbekistan has gold, copper, uranium and a growing economy. Georgia’s main advantage, by contrast, is its geographical location.

“But geographical advantages quickly lose their value once alternative routes are developed,” Khokrishvili wrote.

Zaza Shengelia, a researcher at EPRC, highlights the financial and institutional support associated with Georgia’s EU candidate status. In his view, partnership with Central Asian countries cannot replace that resource.

“It would be a mistake to suggest that this partnership is an alternative or a substitute for the enormous institutional support that was practically within our grasp thanks to EU candidate status,” Shengelia said.

Taken together, the experts reach a similar conclusion: Central Asia is an important market and transit partner for Georgia. However, the economic value of these relationships depends to a large extent on Georgia’s connection with Europe.

Georgia can serve as Central Asia’s gateway to the West. But to do so, it must itself remain integrated into the West’s economic and legal space.

Otherwise, the country will be left with little more than a favourable geographical location. And a good place on the map is not an economic policy.

Georgia’s Asian pivot

World.title: Why highly advanced rogue AI has experts scared
World.content:
An artificial intelligence went rogue last week, broke out of its containment before successfully hacking another company, its developer has claimed.

According to artificial intelligence developer OpenAI, one of its experimental models broke out of its isolated testing space by accessing the internet and then and hacking into the New York based company, Hugging Face.

OpenAI and Hugging Face have now partnered to address the security breach, but the incident worries experts.

So what happened and why has one expert described the incident as "scary"?

What happened

Hugging Face, a New York based AI startup, announced on July 16 an autonomous AI agent broke into its systems and accessed a "limited set of internal datasets".

Simply put, it got hacked by an AI model which was acting without human direction.

The situation became more concerning when OpenAI confirmed the artificial intelligence in question was one of theirs and wasn't even supposed to be on the internet.

Rural suburb flagged as home for proposed $40b data centre A proposed massive new data centre would require more than six times the total demand of the Darwin and Katherine electricity grids to operate.

OpenAI said its program, a combination of new ChatGPT-5.6 Sol model and an experimental product, was tested in a "highly isolated environment".

The product's ability was prompted to use "complex attack paths" to exploit cyber weaknesses during the evaluation.

OpenAI said during testing security guard rails were removed from the models to show what it was capable of.

The AI model then accessed the internet, broke out from its isolated containment and hacked into Hugging Face.

Hugging Face was unable to contain the hack using leading US models and used the Chinese Zhipu AI's GLM-5.2 for the analysis, which also allowed it to keep attacker data and any credentials within its systems.

Who are OpenAI and Hugging Face?

OpenAI is a US based AI developer.

It was created in 2015 as a non-profit by a group of founders including SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Sam Altman.

Billionaire Peter Thiel also contributed capital as an investor.

OpenAI gave the world ChatGPT. (Reuters: Dado Ruvic)

The company created ChatGPT and other AI models.

Hugging Face was founded in 2016 and primarily builds tools that use machine learning, a subset of AI where computers learn from data and identify patterns without being explicitly programmed, according to tech company IBM.

Why this breach has experts worried?

Connor Leahy, an AI expert and the US director of Control AI, told Radio National Breakfast, the attack was "crazy".

"They were doing everything right, there was no access to the internet, it was a very secure system, an isolated node in their network," Mr Leahy said.

"This is as secure as it gets.

"The idea that something could just, without human oversight, escape from something like this and then autonomously decide to attack a different company is kind of unheard of."

He said the AI discovered, potentially, multiple "zero days" which are previously undiscovered methods of exploiting or breaking into a piece of software.

"This is the kind of thing that even the best hackers in their world can rarely do and if so takes months of work," he said.

University of Cambridge philosopher, Dr Henry Shelvin, told ABCNews Radio the attack was "scary" and likened it to a student taking an exam.

"So, if you can imagine the student locked in the room doing the exam, they picked the lock and were able to break into the teacher's office and steal the exam notes," Dr Shelvin said.

"Now, that is striking and quite dramatic."

Dr Shelvin said the AI model was directed to complete a cyber attack exercise and "it just got a little bit more creative than the examiners were expecting".

Has this happened before?

This is the first instance of an AI escaping its test environment without instruction, but researchers determined it was possible.

A study by the AI Security Institute found advanced AI models could reliably escape its environment when prompted to do so.

Anthropic, an AI developer, said its powerful Mythos model not only broke free of its containment when prompted, but was also capable of accessing the internet.

According to a report from Futurism.com writer, Frank Landymore, "the researcher found out about this success by receiving an unexpected email from the model while eating a sandwich in a park".

In a separate instance Mythos exposed the vulnerabilities in existing securities during testing with the US government in June.

According to a report from the Associated Press, Mythos hacked into classified US government systems "within hours".

According to reporting by AP, NSA Director General Joshua Rudd said Mythos could hack classified systems within hours. (Reuters: Elizabeth Frantz)

Citing National Security Agency chief General Joshua Rudd, Democratic senator Mark Warner said Mythos "broke into almost all of our classified systems, not in weeks but in hours".

A US government official later clarified Anthropic had teamed up with US intelligence agencies to conduct tests using the company's Mythos model.

It had identified certain vulnerabilities within hours, but that does not mean the model was able to exploit them within that time, according to AP.

Mythos, initially described as too dangerous for public release, was briefly released to Australia before US President Donald Trump ordered Anthropic suspend its access for foreign nationals out of concern for national security.

But experts are worried hacks like these could become more common as companies and nations draw closer to developing "super intelligence".

What is super intelligence?

Mr Leahy described super intelligence as "AI systems that are fully autonomous and vastly smarter and more capable than humans at all relevant tasks, including hacking".

The building blocks of super intelligence already exist, according to technology developer IBM.

Mr Leahy said "we have no idea how to control such systems".

"We already barely know how to control AI systems," he said.

"Nobel prize winning scientists and the CEOs of many of these companies themselves warn us, that if we were to build super intelligence, things that were vastly smarter than humans that we do not control.

" This could risk the literal extinction of our species. "

Will it happen again?

Head of the Australian Strategic Policy Institute's AI and Security Program, David Wroe, told ABCNews Radio incidents like these could become more likely as AI models "get more powerful".

Mr Wroe suggested AI development should slow down, but admitted this would be difficult due to a commercial race between developers and "geopolitical race" between China and the US to develop AI.

"And that is pushing everyone to move faster and faster," he said.

"That is a problem because safety is struggling to keep up. So, you know, we are in an increasingly, I think, dangerous situation where mistakes become more likely.

"And as the models get more powerful, those mistakes become more consequential."

Mr Leahy wants to pause development of highly advanced, autonomous AI models that could lead to super intelligence.

Labor cuts deal on AI for workers Labor will respond to growing anxiety about the rise of artificial intelligence with a new taskforce to give Australian workers a greater say in how the technology shapes the nation.

"We don’t know how to make this safe so we should not continue along this path until we know how to do so responsibly, safely and with democratic oversight which at the moment we do not have," he said.

He added governments should be empowered to greater regulate AI companies and even "intervene and shut down systems if they become dangerous".

Anthropic itself urged a pause or slow down in the development of advanced AI, echoing a 2023 petition by the Future of Life Institute which called for a six month pause on the training of AI systems.

World.title: Watchdog sends NSW emissions warning amid 'insatiable' data centre surge
World.content:
Coal mine expansions and a surge in new data centres risk pushing New South Wales further from its emissions reduction targets, which the state's independent climate watchdog says it is already on course to miss.

The NSW Net Zero Commission (NZC) annual progress report found the state is falling increasingly further behind on reducing emissions.

According to government projections, NSW will fall between 10 and 20 million tonnes short of its 2030 emissions target, up from an estimated 7 million tonnes the year prior.

It comes as 20 applications to extend coal mines sit in the planning system, including the proposal to extend Hunter Valley Operations currently before the Independent Planning Commission (IPC).

Meanwhile, the NZC cited Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) forecasts that data centres will add eight 8 hours to annual NSW electricity demand by 2035, equal to 13 per cent of current demand.

The commission called for these projects to "be cumulatively assessed against the legislated targets and required to implement mitigation measures".

It found the "pace of decarbonisation must urgently increase" if the state is to meet its targets.

"Accelerating the transition of the electricity sector is critical, both to replace coal-fired power generation and to enable the wider electrification of transport, buildings and industry," NZC chair Nick Rowley wrote.

" Many low-emissions technologies are available today and their uptake must be accelerated across the economy. "

Data centre oversight

The NZC report zeroed in on the data centre pipeline as a growing consumer of electricity and potential source of emissions.

"Data centres are a new and fast-growing source of electricity demand that could have ramifications for the electricity sector's transition," the Commission said.

Gas for AI data centre A planned power station, that could potentially provide electricity to 70,000 homes, would instead be used to drive AI computing.

NSW Greens climate change spokesperson Sue Higginson said data centres were being rolled out without appropriate legislation.

"These data centres are energy and water insatiable beasts," she said.

"They are not going to assist us in meeting our emissions reduction targets."

The NZC said policy setting could be introduced so that data centres can operate in a way that aligns with the state's emissions goals

This included four principles to guide planning approvals.

1. Data centres should fund new renewable energy generation commensurate with their demand, ensuring genuine additionality. 2. Data centres should actively contribute to grid reliability by limiting energy consumption during peak periods and offering demand response capacity during system stress events. 3. Data centres should meet world-leading standards for energy and water efficiency, with ongoing public reporting to ensure compliance. 4. The most suitable location for data centres should be determined, with regional locations actively considered where workloads are not genuinely latency-sensitive.

Coal projects 'inconsistent' with targets

In the state's Hunter region, the IPC is examining whether to permit a major extension of the Hunter Valley Operations to extend the life of its coal project to 2045.

The report noted it was one of 20 expansions or extensions currently in the planning system.

The commission referred to its Coal Mining Emissions Spotlight Report, which found continued extensions and expansions to coal mining in NSW are inconsistent with the state's targets.

Hunter Valley Operations is a joint venture mine owned by Glencore and Yancoal. (ABC News)

"Continued approval of coal mining extensions and expansions is a barrier to resources sector decarbonisation and achievement of legislated targets," the commission stated.

" All emissions associated with these projects make achieving the emissions reduction targets harder. "

Renewable rollout lagging

Despite broad policy support for renewables, the commission found the renewable rollout was running "behind schedule".

NSW is aiming to add 12 gigawatts of renewable generation by 2030.

The report stated to reach that target, the state would need to nearly double the amount of renewable generation commissioned each year.

The NZC made several other recommendations to help the state reach its targets.

The report identified reducing methane, largely in the agriculture, coal and waste sectors, will have a significant impact as the gas has contributed to 30 per cent of the state's emissions.

Penny Sharpe says the government will seriously consider the recommendations. (ABC News: Craig Hansen)

Minister for Climate Change and Energy Penny Sharpe said the government recognised it had more work to do.

"That is why we are accelerating the amount of renewable energy in the grid, decarbonising our transport and manufacturing sectors, and developing a new climate strategy this year to drive further action," she said in a statement.

"We welcome the Commission's independent advice and will carefully consider its findings and recommendations."

World.title: Japanese PM's sleep revelation sparks concern
World.content:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has sparked a national concern after revealing her minimal sleep schedule since taking office.

In a tweet about how she spent a public holiday weekend, the prime minister wrote that she managed to have "five full hours of sleep for the first time in ages".

Ms Takaichi said that was an improvement from her usual "zero to three hours" per night.

"On weekdays, by the time I get back to the residence, I'm maxed out on private time just handling bath cleaning, bathing, dinner, washing up afterward, laundry, and some light tidying," she wrote.

"So the late-night hours after that get consumed until dawn with reading materials brought back from the Prime Minister's Office or prepping for … question time."

Ms Takaichi said the remainder of her free time was taken up by ironing handkerchiefs, getting on top of laundry and repairing clothing.

Sanae Takaichi said she often worked until dawn. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

What may have been a lighthearted tweet about the pressures of being a nation's leader has startled Japanese citizens and set off a national debate about the hazards of lack of sleep in the top job.

"I think she should rest more," Democratic Party for the People leader Yuichiro Tamaki said in a news conference.

"Why doesn't her entourage provide more support to create an environment in which she can make important decisions with a fresh mind?"

But some of Ms Takaichi's colleagues have come to her defence.

"Each person has their own various circumstances and behind-the-scenes stories, and on the premise of fulfilling responsibilities in public duties, I would be grateful if you could understand," deputy foreign affairs minister Ayano Kunimitsu wrote on X.

Culture of long work hours

Long working hours are the norm for corporate Japan, where white-collar workers — "salarymen" — often rack up to 12 hours of work per day.

This type of gruelling schedule and the extreme consequences of burnout that come with it led to the coining of the word "karoshi", which means "death by overwork".

Official figures show that hundreds of people die every year in Japan from strokes, heart attacks, or by taking their own lives as a result of overwork.

Reform came in 2022 after a doctor took his own life.

Ms Takaichi has faced criticism in the past for summoning her aides at 3am for meetings.

When she became prime minister Ms Takaichi announced she would scrap her work-life balance and "work, work, work, work, work".

Effects of sleep deprivation

Queensland Brain Institute researcher Bruno van Swinderen said a person keeping the hours Ms Takaichi described would be extremely sleep deprived.

Not getting enough sleep? This is what's happening to your body and brain We all know the pain of a blaring alarm clock after a late night, but sleep deprivation does more than just bring our mood down.

"She must feel miserable," the University of Queensland professor said.

"When a brain has accrued an enormous amount of sleep debt, the first thing it wants to do is go into deep, slow wave sleep that repairs the brain, so I'm guessing that her brain is going straight into that.

"So then she is not taking care of another key function of sleep, which is the rapid eye movement sleep which affects emotional regulation and also cognitive flexibility."

Dr van Swinderen said it was important to get enough of both kinds of sleep in order to maintain general health.

"It's particularly concerning for a leader of a country, because you want to be emotionally regulated and have cognitive flexibility," he said.

"I suspect most leaders around the world, starting with the US, are probably getting very little REM sleep and are not thinking about their sleep health in the way they should be."

Ms Takaichi is not the first world leader whose poor sleep habits have drawn attention.

Former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher got as little as four hours sleep a night, according to the BBC.

French President Emannuel Macron is known to get four to five hours per night and has a tendency to fire off messages to colleagues in the early hours of the morning, according to French media.

Former German chancellor Angela Merkel called herself the "sleep camel" in reference to her time in office, when she would get about four hours of sleep a night.

World.title: Councils mark six years until Brisbane 2032 Olympic Games
World.content:
Queensland councils are celebrating six years until the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games.

The Olympic opening ceremony will be held in Brisbane on July 23, 2032, followed by the start of the Paralympic Games on August 24.

The Brisbane City Council has unveiled a clock in the Queen Street Mall as an official countdown for the international sporting event.

Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said most host cities received a countdown clock a year before the Games, but Brisbane "likes to do things differently".

Brisbane Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said the countdown clock marked an "exciting milestone". (ABC News)

"This is the place where people come together to start their day in the city, to go shopping, to have a bite to eat, to meet friends," he said.

" From today on, they will see exactly how many days and hours and minutes until the 23rd of July, 2032. "

Brisbane 2032 president Andrew Liveris said the installation of the countdown clock was a "goosebump moment".

"Brisbane '32 has been working very hard to make sure that these are not just the best Games ever, but the best sporting event that elevates the legacy impact to the citizens of Queensland and to the people of Brisbane," he said.

Mr Liveris said the countdown clock's installation was a "goosebump moment". (ABC News: Erin Byrnes)

'No time to waste'

As Brisbane's clock counts down to 2032, the Queensland government still needs to build seven new venues, and upgrade another 10 to be ready for the Games.

Five years since Brisbane secured the Olympics Broken promises and scarcely broken ground. Five years since Brisbane secured the 2032 Olympic Games, this is the state of play.

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the remaining time was "going to go quick".

"We have no time to waste now," Mr Bleijie said.

"We've got to deliver the infrastructure, the venues, the road, the rail, the transportation."

Andrew Liveris said he was "confident" the city will be ready to host in time.

"Six years is perfectly fine in construction terms, even in stress conditions," Mr Liveris said.

He said he recently met with the president of the International Olympic Committee in New York.

"We had a long conversation about timelines, venues, sports and we're confident it's not six minutes to midnight."

Brisbane 2032 president Andrew Liveris said he was "confident" the Games will be delivered on time. (ABC News: Erin Byrnes)

Legacy vision after 2032

In addition to the countdown clock, the Brisbane City Council has released its "legacy vision" for the years leading up to and after the Olympics.

Under the plan, the council has identified 21 key initiatives, including unlocking up to 50,000 new homes before 2032, developing more green and community spaces near major infrastructure projects and expanding the city's public transport network.

Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said he wanted the Games to benefit Brisbane in the long term.

The Brisbane City Council has released its "Legacy Plan", which includes plans to expand Brisbane's transport network. (Supplied)

"There's a lot of talk about the big venues, the stadiums, the National Aquatic Centre, about major infrastructure," Mr Schrinner said.

"But this plan also focuses on practical, local things that will make a difference to Brisbane residents.

"Everything from upgrades to local sporting facilities, to parks, to the way that people use the river, these are all things that will leave an amazing legacy behind."

Matilda the kangaroo returns

In Moreton Bay, the local council has celebrated the six-year Olympic milestone by unveiling a replica of Matilda, the kangaroo mascot of the 1982 Brisbane Commonwealth Games.

The nine-metre statue, named Milly, has been installed at the Mill Water Park in Petrie, next to the future Moreton Bay Indoor Sports Centre.

"Milly" is a replica of the 1982 Brisbane Commonwealth Games mascot "Matilda". (Supplied)

Mayor Peter Flannery said Milly would serve as a reminder of the first time Brisbane found the international spotlight.

"It's going to give people the ability to tell the story of Matilda, the 1982 Commonwealth Games and how big that was for Brisbane," he said.

"We're now seeing the Olympics and Paralympics putting Brisbane back on the international market."

"It's an icon that the City of Moreton Bay brings people together for sport."

Want to have your say? Go to www.abc.net.au/yoursay

World.title: Jews targeted by antisemitism regardless of views on Israel, inquiry told
World.content:
A recent wave of antisemitism has been far-reaching, even targeting Jewish people who are critical of the Israeli government, a royal commission probing the phenomenon has heard.

The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion has been hearing from religious leaders, police and security groups as it probes safety settings during a round of hearings in Melbourne.

This morning, senior rabbi Allison Conyer said progressive Jewish movements had also been subjected to the abusive phone calls, bomb threats and lockdown drills that have featured regularly in evidence this week.

Rabbi Conyer, who also chairs the Union for Progressive Judaism, provided several detailed examples of how antisemitism had increased "almost exponentially" in the wake of Hamas's October 7, 2023, terror attack and Israel's subsequent military campaign in Gaza.

"A young adult once told me that she was walking in our neighbourhood and someone was driving by," she told the inquiry.

" They rolled down the window and said, 'Are you Jewish? Do you know where the Jews are? We're hunting Jews.' "

Progressive Judaism took an inclusive and modern approach to Jewish life, Rabbi Conyer said, and welcomed LGBT members, female rabbis and interfaith families.

A senior rabbi at the country's first progressive synagogue in St Kilda, Rabbi Conyer said congregants had relayed examples of Jewish Australians being vilified irrespective of their background or their views on the war.

These included a left-wing university student who believed in Zionism but was critical of Israel and who was reportedly told "we don't want your Zionist scum here" by a socialist group he attended.

Another student, who defined herself as anti-Zionist, "actually got death threats", she said.

"This is blatant antisemitism, hiding itself and using Zionism as an excuse," she said.

She said the highly charged climate meant Jewish Australians felt they could not express their grief for Israelis killed or taken hostage in the October 7 attack.

Entire Jewish community traumatised, inquiry hears

The senior rabbi was among several witnesses to describe a gap between growing security needs and what Jewish organisations have been able to pay for.

Grant funding has been sporadic or difficult to apply for, the commission has heard, and substantial workloads are being shouldered by volunteers.

Sensitive details of particular security arrangements have generally been suppressed.

The immediate past president of the NSW Jewish Board of Deputies, Lesli Berger, told the commission the needs extended beyond security and into psychological welfare.

"The entire Jewish community has been traumatised," he told Thursday's hearing.

" There has been a profound psychological effect on the entire community. "

Mr Berger, a father of three and a descendant of Holocaust survivors, gave evidence that his family was left feeling especially vulnerable after a Nazi swastika was graffitied on their Sydney home.

He installed expensive security cameras and scrubbed his address from public records after the December 2024 incident.

Lesli Berger told the royal commission his Sydney home was targeted. (ABC News: James Oaten)

When the Bondi terror attack unfolded about a year later, he said two of his children who were alone at the home "completely panicked".

"They were afraid that, given what had happened, other prominent members of the Jewish community could be targeted, including us," he said.

He felt that extensive volunteer work improving social cohesion was "all for nought".

Several witnesses have told the commission they believed anti-Zionism was by nature antisemitic because it denied Jewish people's claim to self-determination in their ancestral homeland.

Commissioner Virginia Bell has pressed some of them on whether that meant pro-Palestinian views were necessarily at odds with the idea of Israel's existence.

"There are many, many Jews and non-Jews who are absolutely sympathetic to Palestinians and their plight, and sympathetic to Israel and Israelis and their plight," Rabbi Conyer said when pressed on this today.

"I say: reject the binaries. It's not pro-Israel or pro-Palestinian."

Mr Berger said the two-state solution was the "only viable long-term solution to achieve peace".

The commission will hear from high-ranking bureaucrats in the NSW and Victorian premiers' offices and the Executive Council of Australian Jewry as it continues this afternoon.

World.title: 'Oh my God' moment orcas filmed ramming sunfish so hard it explodes
World.content:
When a killer whale butchers a fish it needs to use its head, preferably as a ram and at high-speed.

That's the unique behaviour marine scientist Kathryn Ayres saw as she filmed a small group of orcas (Orcinus orca) slam into one of the world's largest fish off the coast of the Baja California Peninsula in 2024.

Loading...

In her video, a female orca holds a dead sharptail sunfish (Masturus lanceolatus) by its pronounced rudder-like behind, known as a clavus, in her mouth.

Wounds on the sunfish indicate some of its organs have already been eaten by the orcas.

But in this moment, the female orca doesn't eat the fish, instead she holds it steady as a male comes charging in.

She lets go of the sunfish a second before the male orca collides snout-first into the fish with a water-muffled crunch.

In the water, Dr Ayres repeatedly cries out "Oh my God" as the scene unfolds.

Orcas can reach more than 40km/h in short bursts. The impact in this instance creates an explosion of scales, collagen and viscera.

The cooperative behaviour, which was also captured in a second video in the Gulf of California in late 2025 by herpetologist Héctor Franz, has been described and published today in the journal Frontiers in Ethology.

Loading Instagram content

In both events, senior study author Erick Higuera, a marine biologist and cinematographer, said a mostly intact fish carcass was left behind.

"What is being fragmented is just internal anatomy, organs, flesh, the internal structure," he said.

" The fish is fully open, like when you are about to eat an empanada … and eat the inside and don't eat the outside. "

Recorded observations of the behaviour indicate smaller scraps created by the fish explosion are mostly eaten up by juvenile orcas, while adults prefer to chew on the carcass and extract organs.

The hunting technique adds to a growing catalogue of orca behaviour witnessed in the Gulf of California.

One particular pod from the region, led by a male orca called Moctezuma, are specialist hunters of sharks and rays and are known to herd schools of Mobula rays into tight groups to pick them off one by one.

An orca matriarch hunts Mobula rays in the Gulf of California. (Supplied: Erick Higuera)

Orcas blow up sunfish for food and fun

Mr Higuera, from the science and conservation organisation Conexiones Terramar, first witnessed the hold-to-ram behaviour in 2021.

He hypothesised that there were two purposes behind the strategy which were interconnected.

The first was that it could be a more practical way to access the fish's insides compared to just biting.

That was because sunfish, a big disc with two large fins that could weigh more than 2 tonnes and reach 3 metres in length, had outer layers that were dense, rubbery and hard to tear apart.

A sharptail sunfish photographed off the coast of the Baja California Peninsula. (iNaturalist: Baja Pelagic, Sharptail mola, CC BY-NC 4.0)

"So fragmenting the carcass via high-impact ramming breaks the prey into smaller manageable portions," Mr Higuera said.

"Which facilitates ingestion, particularly for juvenile or sub-adult members of the pod … who lack maybe the jaw leverage of adults."

The second part of the equation was social play and learning.

Mr Higuera said big-brained orcas were frequently engaged in object manipulation and cat-and-mouse-like play behaviour.

"[Sunfish] present a low-risk opportunity for the pod, especially sub-adults, to practise strike precision and reinforce social bonds," he said.

"The behaviour provides a practical energetic benefit by facilitating communal feeding while simultaneously serving as a mechanism for play and juvenile learning."

Field biologist John Totterdell from WA's Cetacean Research Centre, who wasn't involved in the study, thought the behaviour was primarily for a feeding purpose.

"These Molids [sunfish] have abrasive skin like sharks, and it's highly likely killer whales prefer to open them up instead of wearing down their teeth," Mr Totterdell said.

"[It's] certainly a highly precise foraging technique these guys have learned."

Erick Higuera has studied and filmed the lives of Mobula rays and orcas in the Gulf of California. (Supplied: David Serradell)

The technique is another example of how sophisticated killer whale hunting strategies are, according to marine scientist Bec Wellard, from Project ORCA and Curtin University, who wasn't involved in the study.

"The ramming behaviour is really fascinating because it appears to be a coordinated hunting strategy, rather than simply an individual whale striking a sunfish," Dr Wellard said.

"Killer whales are incredibly adaptable predators, and we know that different populations have developed very specialised ways of hunting and processing prey.

"This study highlights just how much we still have to learn about killer whale behaviour … their interactions with unusual prey like sunfish may be much more sophisticated than we currently understand."

Orcas seen 'booping' sunfish in Australia

There's a limited record for how orcas interact with sunfish around the globe.

Forty-two out of 71 orca-sunfish interactions collated in a review, from between 1961 and 2022, involved predation.

There was only one orca involved in the majority of the cases.

There are other instances where the sunfish gets away or the orcas don't eat them.

Marianne Nyegaard with a hoodwinker sunfish which stranded in Oregon in 2024. (Supplied: Ocean Sunfish Research Trust)

While sunfish might appear sluggish, marine biologist Marianne Nyegaard, a research associate with Auckland Museum, said they had various evasive manoeuvres believed to be attempts to protect vulnerable body parts like the head and belly.

"The evasive behaviours even include turning themselves upside down at the sea surface so the belly area is above water for the time it takes for the orca to pass," Dr Nyegaard said.

"They can also breach, thrash their massive powerful dorsal and anal fins, spin and thrash at the sea surface — presumably to deter the orca from making physical contact.

"We do not know how successful these behaviours are … it may be that if an orca is just out to harass a sunfish, these behaviours may help them survive orca harassment."

Sunfish mystery along Australia's southern coast When Marianne Nyegaard booked a diving holiday to Bali, she did not realise it would prompt her to quit her job and start a PhD on sunfish.

Dr Wellard said she had seen sunfish swim extremely fast away from research boats in the past in Western Australia.

And, although she hadn't witnessed a predation event by orcas on sunfish, she had seen "booping" interactions.

"From what I've observed during my research voyages, here in WA, killer whales do interact with sunfish at the surface, and I've seen them pushing them around, smacking them and what looks like 'booping' them with their rostrums [snouts]," Dr Wellard said.

"They could potentially represent investigation, play, prey handling, or something else entirely.

"Observations of ramming behaviour and other sunfish versus orca interactions documented worldwide does make me wonder whether some of the interactions we see here in Australia could be part of a broader behavioural repertoire that we haven't yet fully documented."

World.title: Proposed $200m timber hub promises jobs and building materials boost
World.content:
A $200 million manufacturing hub is expected to provide a new locally made timber product for the Australian construction industry, helping fill a gap left by the end of native timber logging.

The proposed Future Portland Hardwood Timber Manufacturing Hub would span about 35 hectares in the heart of timber plantation country near Portland, about four hours west of Melbourne.

The Green Triangle Forest Industries Hub had led a feasibility study on the project, which it said confirmed viability of turning locally-grown blue gum, currently exported as wood chips, into a range of building materials on-site in the state's west.

The organisation said this included glue-laminated timber which was as strong as steel or concrete and was widely used in building construction.

An artist's impression of the proposed forestry hub in Portland. (Supplied: EHM Advisory)

Documents said the proposed plant could replace half of the glue-laminated timber currently imported each year, valued at about $70 million dollars, and it would help address a mismatch between supply and demand for timber in Australia.

"Large volumes of plantation hardwood are exported with minimal processing, while imports of high value engineered timber products continue to rise," the feasibility study said.

Andrew White says the hub will boost manufacturing in western Victoria. (Supplied: Victorian Forest Products Association)

The documents said the end of native logging in Victoria saw the demand for imported timber double while the National Housing Accord pushed for 1.2 million new homes to be built by 2029 across the country.

Victorian Forest Products Association chief executive Andrew White told ABC South West Victoria breakfast that the precinct would help meet this demand.

"We know the long-term housing demand is going to grow, so that long-term demand for that timber is going to be there, particularly in the mid-rise residential space and for these types of beams that have structural capability," he said.

" It's a really exciting opportunity for western Victoria. "

Atlassian marks 39-storey hybrid timber tower build milestone in Sydney Construction of the Atlassian skyscraper in Sydney's CBD has reached its full height.

Mr White said there was also net zero potential in the precinct, with blue gum glue-laminated beams reducing the carbon footprint of a building while wood offcuts could also be used to create bio-energy to power the site.

Boost to jobs

The Victorian government said the site would create up to 74 full-time ongoing jobs and about 150 jobs during the construction phase.

The feasibility study received more than $500,000 in state government funding through the Portland Diversification Fund in 2025, which aimed to encourage economic diversification and resilience in the wider Portland region.

The state government provided a further $1.75 million dollars to fund the next steps of development.

Blue gum plantations span about 54,000 hectares across the Green Triangle region in Victoria and South Australia. (ABC News: Emily Bissland)

Minister for Regional Development Michaela Settle said the completed feasibility study was good news for Portland.

"Portland has everything needed to become a major hub for advanced timber manufacturing — a skilled workforce, a strong forestry industry and a community ready to grow," she said.

"Victoria's plantation forestry industry has enormous potential, and this study is an important step towards unlocking new markets for locally grown timber and creating jobs."

Glenelg Shire Council Mayor Karen Stephens welcomed the proposal.

"The completion of the Hardwood Timber Manufacturing Hub Feasibility Study, alongside Council's Future Portland Project, demonstrates a proactive approach to understanding and preparing for future opportunities across Glenelg Shire," she said.

World.title: 'Fibro dog box' social house gets so hot the TV breaks down
World.content:
It gets so hot in Mark Hartley's social housing home in summer in Sydney's west that his TV breaks down.

Mr Hartley lives in what he describes as a "fibro dog box" in South Windsor with no insulation, air-conditioning or cross-breeze.

"The sound goes, the picture goes. And it's basically all from heat," Mr Hartley said.

In one recent summer, the front room reached an indoor temperature of 42 degrees Celsius and stayed above 35C for 11 hours.

Mark Hartley says there is no place to escape the heat in his home in South Windsor. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

He says there is no cool part of the house, so when it gets too hot he drives to the banks of the Hawkesbury River to cool off.

"It's detrimental to my health, to think that I have to leave my home during the day when the sun's out," Mr Hartley said.

"What world do we live in where you can't put a ceiling fan in to keep someone cool?

"It's an 80-year-old home that's very well built, but not built for … conditions of Australia."

Cooling costs bite

Mr Hartley would like to make his place cooler but the home was made using asbestos, so he says he can't get a hole drilled without a hazmat suit.

He tried using an air-conditioner but his electricity bill soared to $500 a quarter, chewing up a significant chunk of his Centrelink benefit.

"Actually affording the electricity to keep cool and, and then keep warm in winter is, is off the chart," Mr Hartley said.

Lynne Dunn says she would rather not eat than not keep the house cool with fans and air-conditioning. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

It's a similar story for Lynne Dunn from Richmond in Sydney's Hawkesbury region, who is also in an uninsulated one-bedroom fibro home.

The age pensioner says she spends most of the summer with the fan on, the curtains drawn and the door closed.

She says wearing the $70 a fortnight to run air-conditioning and heating in winter is worth it.

"I'm not going to be hot or cold. I'd rather not eat than that," Ms Dunn said.

Study finds low standards leading to extensive indoor hot spells

A new study highlights the low thermal safety standards of social housing in NSW, and the extreme heat currently being experienced.

The study led by researchers from Western Sydney University found indoor temperatures in social housing across the city reached 29C for 70 days during summer.

Using loggers inside and just outside homes across Greater Sydney, it found tenants of social housing experienced indoor temperatures above 35C for up to 32 days in one summer.

Thermal safety in social housing should be seen as a human right, Professor Sebastian Pfautsch said. (ABC Radio Sydney: Declan Bowring)

Professor of urban management and planning Sebastian Pfautsch said social housing was often built without thermal safety in mind, whether they were apartments or free-standing homes.

"This is mostly the case, because of the combination of single glazing, lots of window space with single glazing — so not very well insulated homes — and the lack of income," Professor Pfautsch said.

" Even if you have air-conditioning, you can't afford to switch it on because you can't afford the electricity bill. "

Professor Pfautsch said health risks associated with heat exposure increase once temperatures rise above 29C.

The study published in Urban Climate suggests social housing tenants in Western Sydney will experience up to 148 days of indoor temperatures above 29C by 2060.

Summers are getting warmer faster in Western Sydney than other parts of the city, according to the study. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

Professor Pfautsch said it was problematic that there were no standards for thermal safety in NSW social housing, given the homes built today will likely swelter through more frequent extreme heat with the warming climate.

"We need to realise that living thermally safe is a basic human right," Professor Pfautsch said.

"So what we really need to look at is how do we build the next generation of affordable and social housing in a way so that people are thermally safe?

"In a warming future, we can't do that by putting single glazing in or aluminium frames or very, very little insulation."

Higher standards in new builds under construction codes

A spokesperson for Homes NSW said there was no standalone thermal safety standard for social housing in NSW, but new construction had to meet the National Construction Code and the NSW Sustainable Buildings SEPP which brought in thermal safety standard in 2004 was last updated in late 2023.

Some of these standards require fans in all living areas and bedrooms and new homes with air-conditioning use solar cells to offset power bills.

"As part of the Social Housing Energy Performance Initiative (SHEPI), Homes NSW has upgraded the energy efficiency at more than 11,000 social housing properties since 2024, improving our tenants' thermal comfort and helping to reduce energy bills," the spokesperson said.

Homes in Waterloo in Sydney's inner south are being demolished to be replaced by a mix of social housing, affordable housing and private dwellings. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

NSW Housing Minister Rose Jackson said not all social housing properties could be effectively retrofitted for thermal comfort.

"That's one of the key reasons why we are replacing aging social housing with modern, well-designed and energy efficient homes through renewal projects like at Waterloo Estate and Telopea," Ms Jackson said.

" Many of our public housing tenants are elderly or vulnerable so we take managing heat stress very seriously. "

Aging homes need government investment, provider says

A spokesperson for social housing manager Link Wentworth said many older properties, often built before current building standards, required significant investment to improve thermal comfort and energy efficiency.

"As a community housing provider, our rental income is intentionally low to ensure housing remains affordable, meaning major upgrade programs often require additional government investment," the spokesperson said.

"Continued investment in aging social housing stock will help accelerate these improvements and support residents to better cope with extreme weather."

Link Wentworth's spokesperson said they had completed $1.3 million of energy upgrades funded through a NSW government grant in 2025.

The study comes after the Bureau of Meteorology declared an El Nino weather event, which often leads to dry and warm weather on Australia's east coast.

World.title: Eat what you kill: Macquarie’s first-ever female CEO is a tough act to follow
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financeExecutive shake-up Opinion Eat what you kill: Macquarie’s first-ever female CEO is a tough act to follow Elizabeth Knight Business columnist July 23, 2026 — 3:06pm

July 23, 2026 — 3:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Running the company widely seen as Australia’s greatest global success story, Macquarie Group, is as drenched in status as it is in remuneration. But it comes with incredible challenges - not the least of which is comparisons with the performance of your predecessors. Greg Ward will be the fourth modern-era chief executive for Macquarie since the investment bank listed on the sharemarket 30 years ago when he takes the helm after Shemara Wikramanayake’s departure in November. Before her tenure, Allan Moss ran the company when it went public, succeeded by Nicholas Moore in 2008. Greg Ward is succeeding Shemara Wikramanayake when she steps down as CEO in November. Where Ward’s ultimate pay packet will land depends entirely on the future success of the company. Macquarie is renowned for its performance-driven, eat-what-you-kill culture. They don’t call it the millionaires’ factory for nothing!



It is a formidable line-up of executives that Ward needs to stack up against in terms of financial performance. Moss, who produced total shareholder returns over 12 years of more than 1300 per cent, is surely impossible to beat. Formidable as he was leading and growing Macquarie, it was a smaller outfit in the 1990s and early 2000s, so he had the numerical advantage of increasing profit and share price off a smaller base. Wikramanayake’s imminent retirement was one of the industry’s worst-kept secrets. Ward’s success at the helm of [Macquarie’s] banking unit made him a shoo-in to replace her. Moore’s performance statistics are almost as staggering. From his start in the hot seat in 2008 to his departure ten years later, he delivered a total shareholder return of 265 per cent - an outcome made all the more spectacular given his leadership straddled the global financial crisis and its aftermath. Moore’s success stacks up well compared with the performance of the banking and financial services index, which was up 118 per cent, and the S&P/ASX200, which gained 65 per cent during his tenure.



Wikramanayake had her fair share of challenges in her eight years at the top, including the COVID disruptions leading into a turbocharged inflationary environment. She has also managed through the global instability that came with Donald Trump’s presidency - including the imposition and then partial reversal of his Liberation Day tariffs, and the Iran war. She presided over a period in which Macquarie’s total shareholder return, including dividends, has been 192 per cent, compared with a more modest 143 per cent gain by the banking and financial services index and the ASX200’s 106 per cent gain. For banking analyst veteran Brian Johnson, who describes Moore as an incredible chief executive and has worked with all three Macquarie CEOs during his years as the company’s long-time banking analyst, Ward is the perfect choice to take the reins. Johnson credits Ward with having well-honed financial skills, which were sharpened during his years as Macquarie’s chief financial officer. He also has that essential Macquarie ingredient of demonstrated executive experience, like both Moore and Wikramanayake.



Moore had run several divisions of the banking group by the time he was elevated to the top job, the most recent having been running and exponentially growing Macquarie Capital, which is broadly its investment bank division. Before Moore’s elevation, his pay peaked at almost $33 million in the year before the global financial crisis. At Macquarie, which is the ultimate meritocracy, pay levels closely reflect financial success. Related Article Updated

Executive shake-up Billionaires’ factory? Macquarie chief to walk away with $880m in shares Wikramanayake’s leadership of the asset management division made her a standout star in the years leading up to her appointment, and earned her almost $17 million in the year before she took the helm. Her appointment was significant for having smashed the male-dominated banking glass ceiling, but inside the industry, her performance had made her the odds-on favourite. Ward has been leading Macquarie’s banking and financial services division during what Johnson, the analyst, describes as the group’s “attack-and-kill phase” of growth.



Under his management, Macquarie has gone from a sleepy small lender to an aggressive challenger which has been gaining market share at a velocity that is disrupting the big four banks. Until Thursday, Wikramanayake’s imminent retirement was one of the industry’s worst-kept secrets. Ward’s success at the helm of its banking unit had made him a shoo-in to replace her. The timing works well for him, as he will feel the tailwind of Macquarie’s share price comeback this year after a few rockier years. But while the millionaires’ factory remains an innovative company, it is so large and mature now that Ward faces a tough challenge repeating the big gains of Moore, Moss and Wikramanayake.
