World.title: How Colson Whitehead pulled off one of fiction’s great crime trilogies
World.content:
The Pulitzer Prize-winning author didn’t want his obituary to say he never finished the series.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York City gets the final word in Colson Whitehead’s Harlem trilogy – literally. That’s as it should be, for it’s New York that animates the series more than any single character; the constant but ever-changing playground for his cast of occasional crooks and lovable rogues. Would it be fair, I ask, to call these books an 1100-page love letter to his native New York? “It’s a love letter with a lot of beatings,” Whitehead says. “If the love letter includes beatings, then, sure.” We are meeting on a sunny Wednesday morning at an all-day bistro on the Upper West Side, some 40 blocks south of the main spine of Harlem where Ray Carney, the trilogy’s not-quite-hero, keeps his furniture store. Whitehead has just returned from the Netherlands, where he launched the third and final book in the series, Cool Machine, and is about to embark on a North American tour, with dates scheduled until December. He was also profiled by The New Yorker, a process that required so much time he half-jokingly says he would never do it again. But the 56-year-old is accustomed to the demands of a book launch by now. This is his 10th novel, and today he is arguably the most celebrated living novelist in America; his two Pulitzers for fiction, for The Underground Railroad and The Nickel Boys, made him only the fourth person in more than a century to have won the prestigious prize twice. Whitehead is happy to spend some time on the road marketing his latest ware. “I want the book to do well,” he says. “I’m proud of the trilogy, I’m happy to hustle for it.” Hustlers are at the heart of the Harlem trilogy, which follows Carney, his family and his associates over three decades of criminal escapades in and around the Black epicentre of New York. Every book comprises three novellas, each of which tells a distinct crime caper – typically a heist – that sees Carney pulled further and further into the underworld.



Where the first instalment introduced us to an upwardly mobile furniture salesman battling 1960s racial segregation, and the second a middle-aged family man caught in the crosshairs of New York’s 1970s malaise, the final book shows us Ray Carney in his 50s, with both kids out of home, eyeing retirement from both his straight and crooked enterprises. Colson Whitehead and his wife, literary agent Julie Barer. Getty Images It is also the 1980s. Ronald Reagan is in the White House, and the “greed is good” mantra has taken over the city. Modern-day gentrification is taking place, much to our protagonist’s disgust: young urban professionals begin commandeering the crooks’ preferred drinking hole, Donegal’s, and by the story’s end it has been replaced entirely. “The yuppies had won,” Whitehead writes. And ruefully: “There hadn’t been a stabbing in years.” Without giving too much away, it is fair to say the criminal exploits grow more daring and complex as the trilogy goes on. They also expand beyond Harlem, traversing midtown, the gritty Lower East Side and even Queens - and all the class markers therein. Machine’s opening tale centres on an ambitious heist at the grand Waldorf Astoria hotel, where the looters are aided by the homeless denizens of New York’s subway tunnels. “The first two books are very low-technology affairs in terms of the crimes,” Whitehead says. “One of my friends said, ‘No, you have to go big. It’s the ’80s, so go big’.” Carney’s enduring sidekick Pepper, now 64, owns the masterful second portion of the book, as he becomes entwined in a particularly gruesome mission involving a rare and valuable African mask. The perils of crime have taken their toll on Pepper’s ageing body – consigned to “spend more time pissing than thieving these days” – and his suffering only builds sympathy for the old man dragged into one last job. Ultimately, though, we come back to Carney, whose grief and regret over his cousin Freddie haunt him and drive him into a dangerous entanglement in the closing section. This duality runs through the whole series – is Carney fundamentally an honest man with an occasional side hustle? Or is he now more crooked than straight? Did he fall into vice because of its ubiquity, or did he get addicted to the rewards that only thievery can pay?



Wisely, Whitehead doesn’t want to weigh in. “The reader can judge for themselves,” he says. “At the opening of this book, his store’s a success, he’s a successful fence [someone who sells stolen goods]. The question is, what is next for him at this stage in his life? What does crime mean? What does being a father mean? What’s the sum of all his choices?” Whitehead is matter-of-fact in his responses and, as in his work, doesn’t indulge in purple prose. He is generous with his time, but we’re not here to chit-chat; he forgoes coffee or food, content to sip table water during our hour together. There are some obvious parallels between Whitehead’s biography and that of his creation, Carney. By the end of the trilogy, the character is the same age as the author is now; both men also have a daughter who has left home. Both are utterly products of New York City. Author Colson Whitehead receives the National Humanities Medal from then US President Joe Biden in 2023. Bloomberg That is probably where the similarities end. Whitehead left Manhattan to study at Harvard, and returned to the city to work at The Village Voice newspaper in the ’90s before devoting himself to books and becoming a star. Every writer knows how to hustle, but crime was something he had to study. His research is evident in the book’s rich historical detail – what David Hajdu calls the “rightness” and “evocative precision” of Whitehead’s prose – whether that be sketching 1980s New York or deploying the criminal lingo of the era. For those of us unfamiliar with either, the trilogy is a gateway to further reading: I enjoyed learning about legendary East Village dive bar Downtown Beirut, and I’m certain that being “on the lam” will work its way into my regular vocabulary. It is arguably the funniest instalment in the series, whether in Carney’s depiction of his daughter’s do-gooder white boyfriend (“a nice boy, for a yuppie bastard”), or this account of a character’s new squeeze: “He had introduced her to Club Med vacations and, supposedly, orgasms.”



Whitehead says he knew while writing book one, Harlem Shuffle, that he wanted to craft a trilogy. Before it was published, he planned the final scene of book three, and had time to drop details into the manuscript that would set up plot points in the later books. Still, he did not publicly describe it as a trilogy at the time. ‘There does seem to be a feeling of optimism in the city. But as a lifelong New Yorker, I always know that the crash is coming. So enjoy it while you can.’ “It’s just my personality, I thought, ‘What if I get bored?’” Whitehead says. “I don’t want my obituary to say, ‘He never finished that crime trilogy he talked about in 2019’. I told my friends, but I didn’t tell interviewers.” Editor's pick Literature The hidden magic of re-reading (and why it’s good for your brain) He did not get bored by it in the end. But seven years is a long time to dedicate to one project. I ask Whitehead whether he received any pushback in the literary world over his commitment to a heist series – the old prejudices against crime fiction. Not in the US, he says, though he detected a little scepticism in Europe. “I think they’re more snobby about that kind of stuff.” Not that Whitehead would care: as he points out, he is the proud author of a zombie novel (2011’s Zone One). There are some subtle echoes of today’s political environment in Cool Machine. Carney fires a sales associate after he admits voting for Reagan twice. Pepper mentions his difficulty keeping track of crises in the Middle East. “They never got solved, they just stacked on top of one another.” How does Whitehead personally parse the social and political times we are in? “The world’s in a pretty terrible place. I hope we survive,” he says. He mentions the destruction of the transatlantic alliance, ignoring climate change, rolling back environmental protections, ICE agents shooting American citizens and mistreating immigrants, and Trump trying to rewrite history by editing history at the Smithsonian – a story that was in the Times that morning.



Whitehead sees Trump as both an outlier – a rich celebrity who didn’t have to bend the knee to the Republican Party – and part of the natural cycle of American politics, one that will shift back to the centre. “We never had a left-wing president,” he says. “We’re not a left-wing country, we’re sort of a centrist country.” We move on to the subject of New York, which is in the midst of what might be described as a Hot Girl Summer. It hosted the World Cup, Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce got married at Madison Square Garden, the Knicks are NBA champions for the first time since Nixon. And Mayor Zohran Mamdani is enjoying an extended honeymoon. Colson Whitehead can see himself moving out of New York in the future. Getty Images “People love the mayor, he’s getting things done, he’s much better than our old mayor,” Whitehead says. “There does seem to be a feeling of optimism in the city. But as a lifelong New Yorker, I always know that the crash is coming. So enjoy it while you can.” At 56, Whitehead has lived long enough to witness the boom-bust cycle that underlines the Harlem trilogy and continued thereafter: the 1990s recession, the dotcom boom and crash, September 11, COVID-19. For him, those cycles are an essential part of the city’s nature and charm. Throughout, the vitality of New York as a magnet for artists has never wavered, even if it feels like the endless march of gentrification is making it harder than ever for creatives to eke out a living. “There’s still great, talented people coming to the city, working in the city,” Whitehead says. “They may not be in the West Village or East Village or downtown Brooklyn, [but] they’re in Bay Ridge, or they’re in Bushwick. Some of them are the great-grandchildren of German and Irish immigrants who moved to Harlem, then went to the middle-class and left Harlem, and now 100 years later, their descendants are coming back to Harlem. I love that cyclical nature of the city.” The notion that “the old New York” has been lost – a regular refrain from some jaded city types – is nonsense, Whitehead argues. “If you’re my age and you’re complaining that things aren’t the same, that’s sort of your role as someone who’s getting older. And the fact that you’re not up on what is new and interesting is a testament to its newness and how out of touch you are. And you should be out of touch. I think youth culture is for the kids.”

World.title: From ‘sexist AF’ to skater vibes: Ranking the Commonwealth Games uniforms
World.content:
LifestyleFashionCommonwealth Games From ‘sexist AF’ to skater vibes: Ranking the Commonwealth Games uniforms Damien Woolnough July 23, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With the world still recovering from the fashion goals and pink soccer boots at the World Cup, Commonwealth Games teams are being coy about their opening ceremony uniforms. So far, only Scotland, Australia and New Zealand have been brave enough to reveal their formal attire, with Bermuda offering substantial hints. So, here is the podium placement for the current finalists. Bronze for Team Scotland: Thistle do The divisive Team Scotland uniforms for the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.



Unveiled with enough smoke to stage a reenactment of a Bonnie Tyler music video, Team Scotland’s ceremonial uniforms could have benefited from an even deeper haze. While the men are decked out in Braveheart black tie, with traditional sporrans, fly plaids and kilts designed by Siobhan Mackenzie, the women are given nightclub-ready black heels, skirts that can be hemmed to your personal highlands and sporran-shaped purses. Tennis legend Martina Navratilova summed up the criticisms on social media, commenting beneath a photo of the uniforms: “It’s crazy … sexist AF.” Mackenzie, who designed the women’s uniform for the Gold Coast 2018 Commonwealth Games, and the tartan outfits at Birmingham 2022, focused on traditional rather than contemporary values. “The outfits are classic and timeless, with the tartan very much the focus,” Mackenzie said. “It’s also really important to me that everything is made in Scotland, from the woven cloth to the finished garments and accessories, supporting local textiles and craftsmanship.”



Billie Eder, sports writer, in Glasgow: First up, athletes in high heels? No, thanks. If they want to choose to wear them in their free time, then go for it. But to mandate it as uniform? Uncool. If I can look past the sexism (it’s kind of hard), I think the blue tartan is really cool. Silver for Team Australia: Top of the class The Commonwealth Games uniforms by R.M. Williams for Team Australia. From the ankles down, Team Australia’s uniforms are the envy of the world – or at least the female Commonwealth Games athletes from Scotland. The covetable Craftsman boots with matching belts from R.M. Williams are quite rightly a source of national pride.



The rest of the uniform respectfully touches on private school blazers, in a pleasing hunter green with a promising touch of gold thanks to the team insignia. There’s a playful whiff of the Dubbo Regional Livestock Markets, thanks to chinos and skirts. First Nations design touches peek out of the jacket lining, breast pockets on the mens’ blazers and on hair ties, worn with crisp white shirts ready for Rotarian speech nights. “Designing for Team Australia goes beyond appearance,” said R.M. Williams designer Charles Kennedy. “It’s about capturing pride, identity, and belonging, and creating pieces worthy of the moment athletes represent their country.” Billie Eder, sports writer: Sigh. Am I really going to take down another Australian team uniform (see my previous work)? You bet. For a country known for its exotic wildlife and stunning landscapes, we sure as hell do fall short in the creativity department when it comes to fashion. It would be a different story if we were putting the First Nations designs on the outer – then people could really see a piece of our nation. Gold for Team New Zealand: Sweet as



The Team New Zealand Commonwealth Games uniforms by Kathmandu. Sustainability without sacrificing style is at the throbbing heart of New Zealand’s official uniforms, provided by Kathmandu. The theme is “future nostalgia” with jackets crafted using merino wool, featuring QR codes on the inside pocket that connect competitors to messages of support from home. Wide leg pants and baseball caps have a welcome skater vibe. Unfortunately, skateboarding is not an official event at the Commonwealth Games. The wool weave in the blazer was developed with Woolmark and the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) for maximum wind and water resistance without the use of synthetic coating. Some of the uniform pieces have been made using recycled plastic waste, including car tyres, with those burnouts in Palmerston North finally paying off.



Billie Eder, sports writer: Yeah, NZ is cool, and they know it. The mix between formal and casual hits the nail on the head, and is so refreshing compared with the rigid uniforms from Australia and Scotland. This is kit you can actually see the athletes wearing again. It’s giving streetwear that will cost a pretty penny at a vintage store one day. An album by calyspo band The Talbot Brothers of Bermuda. Ones to Watch, Team Bermuda Only three of the seven athletes representing Bermuda will take part in the opening ceremony, wearing outfits inspired by the calypso band The Talbot Brothers of Bermuda. The three female athletes will wear carnival shirts, trousers and straw hats inspired by the all-male band.



The look is a deliberate move away from Bermuda shorts. “I’ve chosen a uniform depicting The Talbot Brothers,” chef de mission Donna Raynor told Bernews. “That’s how we will be dressed. I’m sure people will say, ‘Oh, no Bermuda shorts’. We’re excited about that.” Make the most of your health with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Pacgold hits copper-gold jackpot under existing SA gold system
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Pacgold hits copper-gold jackpot under existing SA gold system Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd July 23, 2026 — 2:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pacgold Limited soared almost 50 per cent to as high as 16 cents in early trading after revealing it had punched through a substantial high-grade copper-gold discovery at its White Dam North gold project in South Australia. The company’s latest copper riches had previously lain dormant beneath previously drilled shallow oxide gold mineralisation at the project, hinting at a potentially project-wide copper and gold prize emerging at the gold-producing play. Drilling near Pacgold’s White Dam mine has intersected high-grade gold and copper sulphide mineralisation beneath its known oxide resources. Credit: file Pacgold unveiled a plethora of solid copper-gold hits, including a 20-metre hit grading 2.5 grams per tonne (g/t) gold and 0.5 per cent copper from just 58m, featuring a stunning higher-grade core of 6m at 7.5g/t gold and 1.2 per cent copper. Another hole delivered a 10-metre intercept grading 3.4g/t gold and 0.7 per cent copper from 54m, including a 5-metre section at a solid 5.0g/t gold and one per cent copper.



‘The Curnamona Province is now a very high priority copper-gold exploration address with multiple high-quality copper-gold discoveries.’ Pacgold managing director Matthew Boyes The discovery looks to be a major step forward for the company, confirming a high-grade copper sulphide system lurking beneath what it previously thought was an oxide gold-only mineralised system – the focus of all the historical work at site. Pacgold says the new discovery is coincident with a magnetic anomaly that extends for up to one kilometre in strike, leaving plenty of meat on the bone for further exploration. Importantly, the company says its discovery remains open in all directions, with a host of assays from the same program still pending from holes that have returned wide zones of visible sulphides. Pacgold says massive chunks of up to 59m of sulphide mineralisation have been observed in a further five holes from the program, with assays for the visual copper hits yet to be returned.



With only limited deep drilling ever carried out at the project, the discovery of a primary sulphide system at depth opens up a whole new exploration front for the company. Management says multiple other untested magnetic anomalies with similar structural settings exist at its nearby Rolling, White Dam East and Hannaford West prospects. Pacgold managing director Matthew Boyes said: “The Curnamona Province is now becoming a very high priority copper-gold exploration address with multiple high-quality copper-gold discoveries in what is to date still a very underexplored district.” Pacgold’s White Dam project lies just 80km west of the famed Broken Hill mine within the burgeoning Curnamona Province, which straddles the South Australia-New South Wales border. While the province is famous for hosting BHP’s giant namesake lead-zinc-silver deposit, it is increasingly being recognised as an emerging copper-gold region with strong similarities to the Gawler Craton, home to Olympic Dam.



The area has seen a flurry of recent activity, highlighted by Sandfire Resources’ major farm-in deal with Havilah Resources to earn up to 80 per cent of the nearby Kalkaroo copper-gold project in a transaction valued at up to $240 million. The company made its latest discovery while focusing on infill drilling across the project’s existing 102,000-ounce oxide gold resource, which it acquired in late 2025. However, this latest find of a primary sulphide system seems likely to significantly expand the project’s potential. With the rods still turning, a geophysical survey planned and a conga line of assays from visually impressive drill holes on their way to the lab, Pacgold has plenty of news in the pipeline. What started as an exercise to firm up a known gold money churner has quickly unearthed what looks to be a jackpot. As copper prices surge to all-time highs, a copper-gold discovery in Australia’s premier copper-producing region looks like a much bigger prize with significant blue sky. World.title: ‘Terrible idea’: Bennett slams idea of injury clauses in Latrell contract
World.content:
Key points Ex-Eel Talagi says Luai will help Parramatta’s young halves

Panthers facing contract juggle with stars

Latrell Mitchell is battling to play again in 2026

Cameron Murray headlines mounting Rabbitohs injury toll

Wayne Bennett has rubbished the idea that Latrell Mitchell’s next contract should be contingent on how many games the injury plagued superstar plays for South Sydney. Bennett hopes Mitchell can still figure for the Rabbitohs again soon despite nerve damage threatening to end his season and was encouraged by the sight of the 29-year-old completing laps around Souths’ Heffron Park headquarters on Thursday. Loading Mitchell ran around the perimeter of Souths’ training ground as Bennett’s depleted side trained ahead of a game against Melbourne at Accor Stadium on Friday night where their place in the top eight could be on the line. The Rabbitohs are in the wars after a 34-24 defeat to the Raiders, losing captain Cameron Murray and Tallis Duncan to injuries and David Fifita to suspension in a blow to their finals aspirations.



It has also been more than two months since Mitchell last suited up for the club, having missed the entire State of Origin series along the way due to a back issue and a subsequent calf problem. He has since consulted a neurologist over complex nerve damage that has complicated his recovery from those injuries, raising concerns that he may not return to the field for the rest of the season. Latrell Mitchell, pictured in June, ran laps around Heffron Park on Thursday. Steven Siewert Bennett, however, is not ready to accept that fate. Asked whether Mitchell had played his last game for the season, the veteran coach replied: “We don’t know that. It’s a week by week proposition. He’s back out running now so that’s good. We’ll see where that goes. “He wants to play, so it’s not that he’s trying to avoid playing. It’s something we’ve got no control over and he’s got good people around him and experts in their field, so we’ve just got to wait and see now.”



A series of injuries has restricted Mitchell to only 95 games in seven years at Souths, a disappointing return given his importance to the team and estimated $1.1 million salary. Bennett said he had to assume it was just bad luck and does not believe Mitchell could change anything to avoid breaking down. Latrell Mitchell has played only nine times for Souths this season. Getty “I don’t think so. Maybe play a different sport, hey? Pickleball maybe,” he joked. Bennett was more serious in shooting down the suggestion that Mitchell’s next contract contain clauses that could adjust his wages depending on how many games he missed.





Bennett said he would promote rookie forward John Radel to the starting side in place of Fifita, whose attempt to have a dangerous contact charge downgraded at the judiciary failed, resulting in a two-game ban. Ex-Eels prodigy backs Luai signing as Bears table offer to Paulo Panthers five-eighth and former Eels prodigy Blaize Talagi believes Jarome Luai could prove to be a $700,000 circuit breaker for his old club as the Perth Bears target Parramatta captain Junior Paulo to lead their forward pack. Loading Talagi will line up against his old side on Thursday night in the No.6 jersey Luai wore in four premierships with Penrith. Luai’s 2027 shift to Parramatta has divided opinion since his one-year deal was confirmed last week.



Eels coach Jason Ryles defended the Luai signing – Wests Tigers will pay $500,000 of his salary – once again on Wednesday, as Perth stepped up their pursuit of 32-year-old Paulo. The Bears are prepared to offer Paulo a two-year deal after coach Mal Meninga met with the ex-NSW Origin prop. Parramatta have been in talks with Paulo about a one-year extension for some time, and he will now weigh up the added security of the Bears offer against moving his family to WA. Eels veteran Junior Paulo is weighing up an offer from the Bears. NRL Imagery Meanwhile, Ryles insisted Luai’s 12-month pit stop before joining PNG in 2028 won’t undermine Parramatta’s development of playmakers such Lorenzo Talataina, Lincoln Fletcher (both 19) and Joash Papalii (22), and denied it points to a lack of long-term roster planning. Talagi has emerged as an unlikely ally in the debate around Parramatta’s roster, having knocked back a lucrative three-year Eels extension to join Penrith in 2024.



Talagi played fullback, centre and off the bench in his debut season when Dylan Brown and Mitchell Moses were entrenched as Parramatta’s halves, albeit with contract options that allowed Newcastle to poach Brown with a record-breaking 10-year deal. Talagi stressed that playing alongside Nathan Cleary in the Panthers’ title-winning system was the driving factor behind leaving his junior club. Blaize Talagi has backed Parramatta’s signing of Jarome Luai. Wolter Peeters But having been mentored by Luai when playing in the halves for Samoa and touring the UK together, he said Luai’s short-term stint could work out perfectly for Parramatta’s next generation of playmakers. “I don’t see anything but good things coming from signing Romey for Parramatta to be honest, especially the younger guys coming up,” Talagai said. “He’s definitely someone who knows how to lead and lead with his actions, and his record speaks for itself.



“For me when I was at Parra, it was the biggest call of my life to leave, and the club was struggling at the time. “So moving to a club where I could tell there wouldn’t be all the focus on me, knowing there would be older guys, obviously someone like Nath to play alongside, that was a big attraction. “I’ve matured a lot since I’ve been here. I think that’s just natural, but I also think it could have been very different if I’d stayed, too. Being a half in the NRL, there’s pressure that comes with that and I think timing of when you play first grade and how you develop is really important. “You’ve got to be properly prepared, and everyone develops at different times. Even when I first got here, there were no promises and I started in reserve grade. “It ended up being the best thing for me, it gave me extra time to adapt to how Penrith do things, so I don’t think anyone should get too disheartened as a young half.”



Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Joey Manu’s $1.6m contract call signals latest shift in cross-code talent stoush Parramatta have high hopes for Talataina and Fletcher as long-term playmakers. But given they are both still teenagers, the pair are considered another 12 to 18 months away from being ready for the NRL. Ryles bristled at comparisons between the short-term deals of Luai and Broncos-bound half Jonah Pezet, who has been stuck in NSW Cup behind Ronald Volkman recentlt. “Jonah’s an up-and-coming player who’s done a great apprenticeship and is on his path to being a seasoned first-grader, and Jarome is a four-time premiership winner,” Ryles said. “So there’s a little bit of a difference there. I don’t apologise for anything that we’ve done … Is there a fear of [upsetting other players]? No, there isn’t, because we’re sitting in a spot on the ladder that we don’t want to be.



“It’s no one’s fault directly, but we need more experienced players. Jarome fits that bill at the moment. “We have got younger players that are coming through our pathways and our system that may be ready in 12 months. “But this gives them an extra bit of time to give them their reps in [NSW] Cup and learn off a true pro that’s won a lot of premierships.” Penrith typically pause contract talk to win titles. Will this year be any different? Dan Walsh



Ivan Cleary remains unfazed by Penrith’s multimillion-dollar roster juggle revolving around the future of his son and superstar halfback Nathan ahead of a critical few weeks before the club traditionally pauses contract talks to win premierships. Penrith’s 2027 off-contract list has dominated rugby league’s rumour mill all year, with Nathan Cleary’s next contract move key to the Panthers salary cap and 10 NRL squad members who will become free agents if they are still unsigned come November 1. Nathan Cleary’s future has been a talking point all season. Tertius Pickard Cleary was front-page news of The Daily Telegraph on Monday, which declared the game’s best player would test the market. Sources speaking on the condition of anonymity due to the confidential nature of discussions have told this masthead he is yet to decide whether he goes to November 1, and that he will begin giving his future genuine consideration after Thursday’s clash with Parramatta.



Father Ivan said he didn’t know when asked on Tuesday if Cleary planned to test the market, and said he couldn’t “remember the last time” he spoke to his son about his contractual future. Ivan announced mid-year that 2027 will be his last season as head coach, with assistant Peter Wallace anointed as his successor. The Panthers remain confident a long-term extension can be sorted for their prize-winning No.7 to keep Cleary from entertaining rival offers. The club first discussed a new deal with his management at the start of the season and have continued to negotiate with the rest of their roster in the background. Further talks are scheduled with star front-rower Moses Leota after he was recently granted a brief window to negotiate with rival clubs for 2028 and beyond. Underrated hooker Mitch Kenny was the first off-contract Panther to recommit to the club on a lucrative four-year deal last week.



Throughout Penrith’s run to four straight premierships, the club typically paused contract talks leading into the end of the regular season and finals to avoid off-field distractions. No hard and fast rule enforced the policy, but a similar stance looms once another few weeks of negotiations take place, and there is further clarity on Cleary’s future. The Panthers have suffered three of their four losses this season in the past five weeks, but have most importantly come through the Origin period unscathed. Kenny is their only top-line player sidelined through injury, though a return date from his badly broken leg is still unknown.



Focus on the club’s retention’s fight has intensified since Cleary, Isaah Yeo, Liam Martin and Brian To’o’s NSW Origin commitments wrapped up, but Ivan Cleary said contract talk hadn’t proved any more a distraction than previous years. “It is in the background,” Cleary said. “Obviously our GM Shane Elford’s done a lot of work in the background all year, because ideally we don’t want [players] to go to market, but we respect if they do. “I don’t think it’s a distraction any more than any other time…I’m confident it’ll work out the way it’s meant to work out for all of them. I feel pretty confident that we’ll get our share of wins there, and if we don’t, then it won’t be through lack of trying.” Luckless Latrell to see specialist for ‘complex nerve damage’ Adrian Proszenko



Latrell Mitchell may have played his last game in 2026, with the South Sydney superstar consulting a neurologist for treatment on “complex nerve damage” in a desperate bid to return to the field this year. Mitchell’s prognosis is one half of a double blow for the Rabbitohs, with captain Cameron Murray also sidelined for up to a month with a calf injury he suffered in the loss to Canberra. The pair are the highest-paid members of the playing squad and represent about $2 million of talent unavailable to coach Wayne Bennett in the run to the finals. Cameron Murray and Latrell Mitchell, Souths’ highest-paid players, are due for more time on the sidelines. Mitchell’s scheduled return from a back injury last month was aborted after he tore his calf in training. It was hoped Mitchell could be fit for the round-23 clash against Parramatta on August 8, but it’s increasingly likely he has played his last game for the season. This masthead broke the news of Mitchell’s diagnosis on Tuesday, with the club providing a further update later in the day.



“Centre Latrell Mitchell has undergone further investigations and consultation with a specialist neurologist last week,” the club statement said. “Mitchell is trying to overcome complex nerve damage that initially created complications with a lower back injury, and now a calf issue in his left leg. Mitchell will remain a week-to-week proposition as to a return to the field of play.” Latrell Mitchell injured his calf in training last month as he attempted to return from a back injury. Steven Siewert In further bad injury news, centre Tallis Duncan has sustained a hamstring strain that will sideline him for two to three weeks. Latrell Siegwalt will replace Duncan for Friday’s clash against the Storm at Accor Stadium, while Lachlan Hubner comes in at lock for Murray. “Trelly is doing good, he obviously wants to be out there with the boys,” Souths centre Jack Wighton said of Mitchell.



“He’s a presence we’re missing, he’s an awesome player to have on the field with you. He just gives you that confidence and belief. The quicker we can have him back, the better. We can’t wait to have him back, we love big Trell.” Murray and Mitchell are part of an already bulging casualty ward that includes Sean Keppie (thumb, expected return round 23), Dayne Jennings, (knee, TBC) Adam Elliott (ankle, season) and Talanoa Penitani (hamstring, round 26). Murray’s teammates acknowledged the significance of his absence, but believed the team would be able to cover for him. “Huge [loss]. Any team that Cam Murray is playing in, he has a massive positive impact on how they play,” Campbell Graham said. “We are obviously no different. He’s our captain, he’s our leader and he’s one of those blokes who gives you confidence when you’re running out there with him.



Related Article NRL 2026 ‘It’s people’s jobs’: Dragons take aim at costly refereeing calls “He’s a loss for us over the next few weeks or so, whatever it is. As I said before, it takes an NRL squad to do something in this competition and we believe we’ve got the depth. “The boys have filled that position before and done the job for us. We’re still confident we can steer the ship while he’s out and hopefully we’re in a good position when he’s back ready to play.”

Junior Tatola added: “It’s obviously a big loss for us, he does a lot of work. “He’s great to be next to and play with. It’s a big loss, but we have got boys in there that can step up to the plate and do the same job as what came does as well.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Australia’s best romcom comes to a bittersweet end
World.content:
★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview Australia’s best romcom comes to a bittersweet end Jared Richards July 23, 2026 — 2:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Colin from Accounts ★★★★ It’s bittersweet that Colin from Accounts’ third season is its last. The hit Australian romcom, created by and starring real-life couple Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer, has captured hearts around the world for good reason. A sharp balance of rom and com, it’s been distinct and charming right from its first moments – a meet-cute for chaotic Sydney doctor in training Ash (Dyer) and craft brewery owner Gordon (Brammall) involving a nipple flash, a car accident and a shared $12,000 vet bill for a stray border terrier. Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer return for the final season of Colin From Accounts. Binge As a relationship formed around their new wheel-assisted dog (the show’s namesake), Colin from Accounts had an ease to its punchlines and cringe comedy thanks to a lived-in chemistry, plus a delightful balance of sweetness and acidity. Any one of those qualities can be hard to come by in the streaming era’s take on comedy, which tends to lean either absurd or overtly dramatic. The only thing more rare is a show going out on its own terms, which is why it’s difficult to be too upset that Brammall and Dyer announced that “creatively, it feels like the right time” for the series to end.



So where to for Ash and Gordon? Season three picks up in the aftermath of Gordon’s impromptu drunken proposal at Ash’s friend’s wedding on a crowded dance floor. While I’m sworn to secrecy on specifics, it’s safe to say that the gesture wasn’t received well, and we reunite with the couple at a very different place and time in their lives. Related Article Streaming ‘There’s been dumb luck’: Patrick Brammall on Colin, Hollywood haters and what’s next Across the four of eight episodes offered for review, Ash and Gordon find themselves – separately and together – questioning what their magnetic hold on each other means. Is it a sign they’re meant to be? Or the result of two broken and bruised people seeing themselves in the other? Don’t worry, comedy is still at the forefront. Neither Ash’s friend Megan (Emma Harvie) and her new-age partner Rumi (scene-stealer Virginia Gay) or Gordon’s brewery mates (Genevieve Hegney and Michael Logo) have any time for their moping. Other supporting characters remain as eccentric as ever, including Justin Rosniak as Gordon’s ocker brother, and Ash’s overbearing, manosphere-influencer mum (Helen Thomson).
